sections.s6_takeaway:
My approach to optimizing a slow query is measure-first and least-invasive-first, never guesswork. The very first thing I do is reproduce the query and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to get the actual plan with real timings and real row counts. That immediately tells me where the time goes — a sequential scan on a big table, a nested loop over too many rows, a sort spilling to disk, or heavy heap fetches — and a large gap between estimated and actual rows tells me the statistics are stale, in which case simply running ANALYZE can be the whole fix.

From there I apply the cheapest effective change. Indexing is the most common: a composite index matching the filter and the sort, with equality columns first, or a covering index with INCLUDE for a hot projection. Then I rewrite for logical cost — making predicates sargable by removing functions from indexed columns, selecting only the columns I need instead of star, and turning correlated subqueries into joins. For joins at scale I make sure both sides are indexed on the join key so the planner picks a hash or merge join instead of a nested loop, and I filter early to shrink the rows entering the join.

Only when the data itself is genuinely huge do I reach for heavier tools: range partitioning so queries prune to the relevant slice, caching for hot read-mostly results, or schema changes like pre-aggregated summary tables. Adding memory or faster storage is my last resort, because hardware hides an inefficient query rather than fixing it.

At the National Bank of India our account-statement query ran for seconds, and the plan showed a sequential scan plus a disk sort. I refreshed statistics and added a composite index on account and date, and the plan turned into an index range scan with the sort node gone entirely, dropping it to milliseconds. As the transactions table grew toward billions of rows, I added monthly range partitioning so date queries pruned to a single partition. The discipline I always emphasize is to change one thing at a time and re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE after every change, because stacking fixes blindly makes it impossible to know what actually helped, and the execution plan is the only honest proof that the query really got faster.

answers.question: If a table has 2 million records and a query is very slow, how do you optimize its performance end to end?
answers.shortTitle: Optimizing a very slow query on a 2 million row table — end to end

s1_definition.profdef: End-to-end query optimization on a large table is a disciplined, evidence-driven process: you first measure the actual execution plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, identify the real bottleneck (sequential scan, sort spill, nested loop, stale statistics), then apply the least invasive fix first — refreshing statistics, adding or correcting indexes, rewriting the query to be sargable, and only then reaching for structural changes like partitioning, denormalization, or caching.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a ledger book with 2 million transaction lines. Rajesh asks "show me all my transactions in March." If the clerk reads every single line from page one to find Rajesh's March entries, it takes forever. Optimization means giving the clerk an index at the back of the book (go straight to Rajesh's section), keeping the index fresh so it points to the right pages, and asking the clerk a clear question he can answer without scanning everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: Measure first with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, fix the cheapest proven cause, and re-measure after every change.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** End-to-end query optimization on a large table is a disciplined, evidence-driven process: you first measure the actual execution plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, identify the real bottleneck (sequential scan, sort spill, nested loop, stale statistics), then apply the least invasive fix first — refreshing statistics, adding or correcting indexes, rewriting the query to be sargable, and only then reaching for structural changes like partitioning, denormalization, or caching.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a ledger book with 2 million transaction lines. Rajesh asks "show me all my transactions in March." If the clerk reads every single line from page one to find Rajesh's March entries, it takes forever. Optimization means giving the clerk an index at the back of the book (go straight to Rajesh's section), keeping the index fresh so it points to the right pages, and asking the clerk a clear question he can answer without scanning everything.

**One line to remember:** Measure first with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, fix the cheapest proven cause, and re-measure after every change.

sections.s2_technical:
The golden rule is never guess. Two million rows is not large for a database, so if a query is slow the cause is almost always a missing index, a non-sargable predicate, stale statistics, or a bad join order — not the row count itself.

Start by capturing the plan. In PostgreSQL you run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...` which executes the query and shows actual time, actual rows, and whether it read from disk or cache. For example `EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001' AND txn_date >= '2024-03-01';` will reveal if the database did a `Seq Scan on transactions` (bad — reads all 2 million rows) or an `Index Scan` (good).

If you see a sequential scan on a filtered query, add an index matching the filter: `CREATE INDEX idx_txn_acct_date ON transactions(account_id, txn_date);`. Equality columns go first, range columns last, because of the left-prefix rule.

If the estimated rows in the plan differ wildly from actual rows, the statistics are stale. Running `ANALYZE transactions;` refreshes the planner's histogram so it chooses the right strategy.

Make predicates sargable so the index can be used. A predicate like `WHERE YEAR(txn_date) = 2024` cannot use an index because the column is wrapped in a function. Rewrite it as `WHERE txn_date >= '2024-01-01' AND txn_date < '2025-01-01'` so the index works.

Select only the columns you need. `SELECT *` forces the database to fetch wide rows and often prevents a covering index. If you only need the amount, `SELECT amount` lets a covering index answer the query from the index alone.

Only after exhausting indexing and rewriting do you consider structural changes: range partitioning by date so queries prune to one partition, a summary/pre-aggregated table for heavy reports, read replicas to offload analytics, and caching hot results in Redis. Hardware upgrades are the last resort because they hide the inefficiency instead of fixing it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the `transactions` table has grown to 2 million rows. When Rajesh opens his mobile app and taps "Transaction History for March," the screen spins for eight seconds. This is exactly how a missing index behaves — the database reads all 2 million rows to find the few hundred that belong to Rajesh.

Problem 2 — The mobile team wrote the filter as `WHERE EXTRACT(MONTH FROM txn_date) = 3`. This is exactly how a non-sargable predicate behaves — wrapping the column in a function disables any index, so even if an index existed it would be ignored.

Problem 3 — After adding an index, the monthly statement report still occasionally runs slow because statistics are stale after a big import. This is exactly how stale statistics behave — the planner thinks the table is small and picks a scan.

We will build a Spring Boot `StatementService` that queries transactions for an account and date range. The code will show the slow query, the fast indexed query, a sargable rewrite, and the SQL migration that adds the index. The service method `getStatement(accountId, from, to)` will return a list of transactions using a repository method that maps to an index-friendly query.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's account `SAV2001`, date range `2024-03-01` to `2024-03-31`, against a `transactions` table of 2 million rows.

Step 1: The HTTP GET arrives at `StatementController`. Spring binds the path variable to `accountId = "SAV2001"` and parses the two dates. Nothing has touched the database yet.

Step 2: The controller calls `StatementService.getStatement`. The service records a start timestamp so we can log the real duration.

Step 3: The service calls `repo.findByAccountIdAndTxnDateBetween`. Spring Data generates the SQL `WHERE account_id = ? AND txn_date BETWEEN ? AND ?`. Because the column is not wrapped in any function, the predicate is sargable.

Step 4: PostgreSQL's planner sees the composite index `idx_txn_acct_date`. It performs an index range scan: it jumps directly to the `SAV2001` section of the index, then walks only the March entries. Instead of reading 2 million rows, it reads a few hundred.

Step 5: The matching rows are returned to the service. The service computes elapsed milliseconds and logs the row count and timing. The same query that took eight seconds on a sequential scan now returns in single-digit milliseconds.

Step 6: The rows flow back through the controller and are serialized to JSON for Rajesh's app.

sections.s6_takeaway:
My approach to a slow query on a two-million-row table is always evidence first. Two million rows is actually small for a modern database, so if the query is slow the problem is almost never the row count — it is a missing index, a predicate that cannot use an index, stale statistics, or a bad join plan. The very first thing I do is run EXPLAIN ANALYZE with buffers to get the real execution plan with actual timings and actual row counts.

The plan tells me exactly where the time goes. If I see a sequential scan on a filtered query, I add a composite index that matches the filter, with equality columns first and range columns last. If I see a huge gap between estimated and actual rows, the statistics are stale and I simply run ANALYZE, which can be the entire fix. If the index exists but is ignored, the predicate is usually non-sargable because the column is wrapped in a function, so I rewrite it into a plain range comparison.

I apply the cheapest effective fix first and re-measure after every single change, because stacking fixes blindly makes it impossible to know what actually helped. Only when the data is genuinely huge do I reach for structural changes like range partitioning so queries prune to one slice, pre-aggregated summary tables for heavy reports, read replicas to offload analytics, and caching for hot read-mostly results. Hardware is my last resort because it hides an inefficient query instead of fixing it.

At the National Bank of India our statement screen for an account's monthly transactions took eight seconds. The plan showed a sequential scan over the whole table plus a disk sort. I added a composite index on account and date, made the date filter a plain range instead of an EXTRACT function, and refreshed statistics. The plan turned into an index range scan with no sort, and the query dropped to six milliseconds. As the table kept growing I added monthly range partitioning so date queries touched only one partition. The discipline I always emphasize is that the execution plan is the only honest proof that the query really got faster.

---

answers.shortTitle: A query that was 50ms suddenly takes 10 seconds — troubleshoot from evidence

s1_definition.profdef: Troubleshooting a sudden latency regression is a differential diagnosis: the query was fast before and is slow now, so something CHANGED. You gather evidence by comparing the current execution plan to the known-good baseline, checking index usage, statistics freshness, lock waits, parameter skew, data growth, recent schema or deploy changes, and server resource utilization — then fix the specific thing that changed rather than reflexively adding an index.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank's teller used to find Rajesh's record in fifty seconds and now takes ten minutes for the same request. You do not immediately hire more tellers. You first ask: did someone move the index cards? Is another clerk holding the drawer locked? Did the filing cabinet suddenly triple in size? Did someone change the form yesterday? You find WHAT CHANGED, because the request itself did not change — the environment did.
s1_definition.oneliner: A regression means something changed, so compare now versus before and fix the delta — do not reflexively add an index.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Troubleshooting a sudden latency regression is a differential diagnosis: the query was fast before and is slow now, so something CHANGED. You gather evidence by comparing the current execution plan to the known-good baseline, checking index usage, statistics freshness, lock waits, parameter skew, data growth, recent schema or deploy changes, and server resource utilization — then fix the specific thing that changed rather than reflexively adding an index.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank's teller used to find Rajesh's record in fifty seconds and now takes ten minutes for the same request. You do not immediately hire more tellers. You first ask: did someone move the index cards? Is another clerk holding the drawer locked? Did the filing cabinet suddenly triple in size? Did someone change the form yesterday? You find WHAT CHANGED, because the request itself did not change — the environment did.

**One line to remember:** A regression means something changed, so compare now versus before and fix the delta — do not reflexively add an index.

sections.s2_technical:
The key insight is the word "suddenly." The query and its parameters are the same as yesterday, so the query is not the villain. Something in the environment changed, and your job is to find the delta.

First, compare the execution plan now versus the baseline. Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and compare it to the plan you captured when it was fast (this is why teams store baseline plans). If yesterday it did an index scan and today it does a sequential scan, the planner changed its mind — and you need to find out why.

The most common reason the planner changes its mind is stale statistics. After a large bulk load, the planner's row estimates become wrong, so it picks a scan over an index. Running `ANALYZE` refreshes them. You can confirm by looking at the estimated versus actual rows in the plan — a large mismatch points straight at statistics.

Check lock contention. A query can be fast in CPU terms but spend ten seconds WAITING for a lock held by a long transaction. In PostgreSQL `SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';` shows blocked queries and the blocking PID. If the time is spent waiting, no index will help.

Check parameter skew. The same query shape can be fast for one value and slow for another. `WHERE status = 'SETTLED'` might match a thousand rows, but `WHERE status = 'PENDING'` might match two million during a backlog. A cached plan built for the selective value becomes terrible for the non-selective one — this is parameter sniffing.

Check data growth. A table that silently grew from fifty thousand to fifty million rows changes which plan is optimal. Check table size over time with monitoring.

Check recent schema changes and deploys. Did someone drop an index last night? Did a migration change a column type and invalidate an index? Did a new ORM query ship? Correlate the slowdown time with the deploy timeline.

Check resource utilization. If CPU is at 100 percent, disk is saturated, or memory pressure forced sorts to spill to disk, the query is slow because the server is starved, not because of its own plan.

Why "just add an index" is the wrong reflex: if the real cause is a lock wait, an index does nothing. If the cause is stale statistics, adding an index without ANALYZE may still be ignored. If the cause is a dropped index, you want to restore the exact one, not guess a new shape. Adding a random index also adds write overhead and can make things worse. You fix what changed, not what you imagine.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the fraud-check query `SELECT ... WHERE status = 'PENDING'` was a steady fifty milliseconds. This morning it jumps to ten seconds. This is exactly how a regression behaves — the query text is identical, so the environment changed.

Problem 2 — Overnight a batch imported two million new pending transactions during an outage backlog. This is exactly how parameter skew plus stale statistics behave together — the value `PENDING` is now huge, and the planner's old statistics still think it is tiny, so it picks the wrong plan.

Problem 3 — A separate long-running reconciliation transaction is holding a lock on the same table. This is exactly how lock contention behaves — the query spends its ten seconds waiting, not computing.

We will build a `RegressionDiagnosticService` that captures the current plan, compares estimated versus actual rows to detect stale statistics, queries `pg_stat_activity` to detect lock waits, and logs a diagnosis recommending the correct fix (ANALYZE, kill the blocker, or restore a dropped index) rather than blindly adding one.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the fraud-check query `WHERE status = 'PENDING'` that was 50 ms yesterday and is 10 seconds today.

Step 1: The diagnostic service first checks for lock waits by querying `pg_stat_activity`. The data here is the live session list. If any session is waiting on a lock, we stop — an index is irrelevant because the time is spent waiting.

Step 2: If there are no lock waits, the service checks statistics freshness in `pg_stat_user_tables`. The data is the last-analyze timestamp and live tuple count. Overnight two million rows were added and auto-analyze had not yet run, so statistics are stale.

Step 3: The service runs `ANALYZE transactions`. This does not change any row data; it refreshes the planner's histogram so its row estimates match reality again.

Step 4: With fresh statistics, the planner re-evaluates the same query and now chooses the correct plan. The data returned to the caller is a `Diagnosis` object that names the true cause and the correct fix, explicitly marking `addIndexJustified = false`.

Step 5: The diagnosis is logged so the on-call engineer sees the reasoning, not a reflex. The query returns to 50 ms without adding any index.


sections.s6_takeaway:
When a query that was fifty milliseconds suddenly becomes ten seconds, the most important word is "suddenly." The query text and its parameters are the same as yesterday, so the query itself is not the villain — something in the environment changed, and my entire job is to find that delta. That is why "just add an index" is the wrong reflex: if the real cause is a lock wait or stale statistics, an index does nothing, and a random index even adds write overhead that can make things worse.

I start by comparing the current execution plan to the known-good baseline using EXPLAIN ANALYZE with buffers. If yesterday it did an index scan and today it does a sequential scan, the planner changed its mind, and the most common reason is stale statistics after a big bulk load. I confirm that by looking at the gap between estimated and actual rows, and the fix is simply ANALYZE, which can be the whole resolution.

Next I check lock contention through pg_stat_activity, because a query can spend all ten seconds waiting for a lock held by a long transaction rather than computing anything. I also check parameter skew, since the same query shape can be fast for a selective value and terrible for a non-selective one — a cached plan built for PENDING when it was small becomes disastrous once PENDING matches millions of rows. Then I check data growth, recent schema changes and deploys, and server resource utilization like CPU, disk, and memory pressure.

At the National Bank of India our fraud-check query on pending transactions jumped from fifty milliseconds to ten seconds one morning. An overnight outage backlog had imported two million new pending rows, auto-analyze had not run yet, and a reconciliation job was holding a lock. I first confirmed the lock wait and ended that blocking transaction, then ran ANALYZE so the planner stopped underestimating the pending rows, and the query went straight back to its normal latency without adding a single index. The principle I always state is: a regression means something changed, so I compare now versus before and fix exactly what changed.

answers.question: (Scenario) A database query that USED to be fast becomes slow and starts slowing down OTHER, unrelated requests too — why does one slow query drag the whole application down, and how do you fix it? (Every request needs a connection from a small pool, e.g. 10 connections. If one query holds its connection for 10 seconds instead of 50 ms, those connections are tied up, so other requests must WAIT for a free connection — now even fast queries look slow and the whole app feels frozen.)
answers.shortTitle: One slow query drags the whole app down — connection pool exhaustion

s1_definition.profdef: Connection pool exhaustion is a cascading failure where a small number of slow queries each hold their database connection far longer than normal, draining the finite pool so that unrelated, fast requests block waiting to acquire a connection. The symptom is high latency and request pile-up across the whole application, often with low database CPU, because the bottleneck is connection availability, not query compute.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank branch has only ten teller windows (ten connections). Normally each customer is served in fifty seconds and the queue flows. One day a single customer's reconciliation takes ten minutes at a window. One by one, slow customers occupy all ten windows, and now Rajesh, who just wants a fifty-second balance check, stands in a frozen queue. The branch is not out of money or clerks — it is out of free windows.
s1_definition.oneliner: The pool is a shared finite resource, so one slow query that hogs a connection starves every other request behind it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Connection pool exhaustion is a cascading failure where a small number of slow queries each hold their database connection far longer than normal, draining the finite pool so that unrelated, fast requests block waiting to acquire a connection. The symptom is high latency and request pile-up across the whole application, often with low database CPU, because the bottleneck is connection availability, not query compute.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank branch has only ten teller windows (ten connections). Normally each customer is served in fifty seconds and the queue flows. One day a single customer's reconciliation takes ten minutes at a window. One by one, slow customers occupy all ten windows, and now Rajesh, who just wants a fifty-second balance check, stands in a frozen queue. The branch is not out of money or clerks — it is out of free windows.

**One line to remember:** The pool is a shared finite resource, so one slow query that hogs a connection starves every other request behind it.

sections.s2_technical:
A connection pool like HikariCP keeps a small fixed number of database connections, for example ten, because each connection is expensive on the database side. Every incoming request borrows a connection, runs its query, and returns it. When queries are fast, ten connections easily serve thousands of requests per second because each is held for only milliseconds.

The failure begins when one query's holding time explodes. If a query now takes ten seconds instead of fifty milliseconds — because of a missing index, stale statistics, a lock wait, or data growth — it holds its connection two hundred times longer. A handful of such concurrent queries occupy every connection in the pool.

Once the pool is empty, every new request, even a trivial one, must wait for a connection to be returned. HikariCP will block up to `connectionTimeout` and then throw "Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms". Now your logs are full of timeout errors for fast queries that were never slow themselves. The application appears frozen, latency across all endpoints spikes, and requests pile up — yet database CPU is often low, because the connections are idle-waiting on locks, not computing.

To diagnose it: find the slow query first. Use the slow-query log, `pg_stat_activity` to see long-running statements, and your APM. Check HikariCP metrics for connection acquire wait time and look for the "connection not available" messages. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the culprit to learn why it got slow.

To minimize the blast radius: fix or add the right index so the query returns to milliseconds. Add a `statement_timeout` at the database and a `@Transactional(timeout = ...)` in the application so one bad query cannot hog a connection indefinitely. Keep transactions short and never make external HTTP calls while holding a connection or a transaction open, because that holds the connection for the duration of the network call. Consider moving heavy analytics or reporting queries to a read replica so they do not compete with normal transactional traffic. Sizing the pool larger is not the primary fix — a bigger pool just delays exhaustion and can overwhelm the database; the real fix is reducing how long each connection is held.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a reporting endpoint that aggregates yearly transactions used to be quick but became slow after data growth and now takes ten seconds. This is exactly how connection hogging starts — one endpoint holds its connection far too long.

Problem 2 — Rajesh's simple balance check, which takes fifty milliseconds, suddenly times out with "connection not available." This is exactly how pool exhaustion spreads — the fast query is a victim, not the cause, because all ten connections are tied up by the slow report.

Problem 3 — The team's first instinct is to raise the pool from ten to one hundred, but the database then buckles under a hundred heavy queries. This is exactly why pool sizing is not the fix — you must reduce holding time, not increase concurrency.

We will build a `TransferService` with a short, timeout-guarded transaction for normal operations and a separate `ReportService` that routes heavy queries with a query timeout, plus HikariCP configuration showing a sane pool size and connection timeout. We add `@Transactional(timeout = 2)` so a runaway query is cancelled before it can starve the pool.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a pool of ten connections, one slow yearly report query, and many fast balance checks arriving concurrently.

Step 1: Normal state — ten connections serve thousands of fast requests. Each balance check borrows a connection, runs for fifty milliseconds, and returns it. The pool is never empty.

Step 2: The yearly report query degrades to ten seconds after data growth. It borrows a connection and holds it for the full ten seconds.

Step 3: A few more report requests arrive. Each grabs a connection and holds it. Within moments, all ten connections are occupied by slow reports. The pool is now empty.

Step 4: Rajesh's balance check arrives. There is no free connection. HikariCP makes it wait up to the three-second `connection-timeout`. The data at this point is a blocked thread doing nothing useful.

Step 5: The wait expires and HikariCP throws "Connection is not available". The fast query fails even though it was never slow. Across the app, unrelated endpoints pile up and time out. Database CPU is low because connections are stuck waiting, not computing.

Step 6: We apply the fix. `@Transactional(timeout = 2)` cancels any runaway transaction after two seconds and returns its connection. The heavy report is routed to a read replica so it no longer competes with transactional traffic. The pool drains and fast queries flow again.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:21 INFO  TransferService - Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 completed
```

```
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Connection Lifecycle State ──────────────────
  [IDLE in pool] ─borrow─→ [IN USE] ─return─→ [IDLE]
                              │
                      timeout(2s) exceeded
                              ▼
                      [CANCELLED → returned]  (blast radius contained)

  Contract for transfer():
    Pre:  from/to exist, amount > 0
    Post: short txn commits; connection returned within 2s
    Guarantee: a runaway cannot hold a connection indefinitely
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
One slow query drags the whole application down because the database connection pool is a small, shared, finite resource. Every request must borrow a connection from a pool of, say, ten. When queries are fast and held for fifty milliseconds, ten connections serve thousands of requests easily. But if one query starts taking ten seconds, it holds its connection two hundred times longer, and a handful of such queries occupy every connection in the pool. After that, even a trivial balance check cannot get a connection — it waits and then fails with "connection is not available." The fast query becomes a victim, and the whole app appears frozen while database CPU is often low, because the connections are stuck waiting rather than computing.

To diagnose it, I find the slow query first through the slow-query log, pg_stat_activity, and the APM, then I check HikariCP's connection-acquire wait time and look for the "connection not available" messages, and I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the culprit to learn why it degraded — usually a missing or ignored index, stale statistics, a lock wait, or data growth.

To minimize the blast radius, I fix the root query, but just as importantly I add guardrails so one bad query can never starve the pool again. I set a statement_timeout at the database and a transaction timeout in the application so a runaway query is cancelled and its connection returned quickly. I keep transactions short and never make external HTTP calls while holding a connection or transaction open. And I move heavy analytics and reporting queries onto a read replica so they stop competing with normal transactional traffic. I deliberately do not just make the pool bigger, because a larger pool only delays exhaustion and can overwhelm the database — the real cure is reducing how long each connection is held.

At the National Bank of India our yearly report endpoint degraded after data growth and started timing out unrelated balance checks even though the database CPU was low. I moved the report to a read replica, added a two-second transaction timeout on the transfer path and a statement timeout on the database, and fixed the underlying index. The pool stopped draining, and fast requests became responsive again. The principle I always repeat is that the connection pool is shared, so protecting its availability protects the entire application.

answers.question: (Scenario) Database CPU hits 100% during peak traffic — how do you respond (identify the top CPU-consuming queries first, then look for slow queries, missing indexes, full table scans, inefficient joins, excessive query frequency / N+1 from the app, and connection-pool misconfiguration), and why must you load-test after the fix to confirm it actually helps under realistic traffic?
answers.shortTitle: Database CPU hits 100% during peak traffic — how do you respond

s1_definition.profdef: Responding to database CPU saturation under peak load is a prioritized investigation that starts from the top CPU-consuming queries (via pg_stat_statements or Performance Insights), then diagnoses why each is expensive — missing indexes causing full table scans, inefficient joins, excessive call frequency such as N+1 from the ORM, or connection-pool misconfiguration — and finishes with a load test under realistic traffic to confirm the fix actually holds, because a change that looks good on one query can behave differently under concurrency.
s1_definition.analogy: During salary-day rush, the National Bank's back office machine runs red-hot at 100 percent. You do not panic and buy a bigger machine first. You look at the work log to see which task is eating the most effort — maybe one report is being run ten thousand times because each customer lookup accidentally triggers a fresh search. You fix that one, then you simulate another salary-day rush to make sure the machine stays cool under the real crowd, not just for one quiet test customer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the top CPU queries first, fix the biggest offenders, then load-test under realistic peak to prove it actually holds.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Responding to database CPU saturation under peak load is a prioritized investigation that starts from the top CPU-consuming queries (via pg_stat_statements or Performance Insights), then diagnoses why each is expensive — missing indexes causing full table scans, inefficient joins, excessive call frequency such as N+1 from the ORM, or connection-pool misconfiguration — and finishes with a load test under realistic traffic to confirm the fix actually holds, because a change that looks good on one query can behave differently under concurrency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** During salary-day rush, the National Bank's back office machine runs red-hot at 100 percent. You do not panic and buy a bigger machine first. You look at the work log to see which task is eating the most effort — maybe one report is being run ten thousand times because each customer lookup accidentally triggers a fresh search. You fix that one, then you simulate another salary-day rush to make sure the machine stays cool under the real crowd, not just for one quiet test customer.

**One line to remember:** Find the top CPU queries first, fix the biggest offenders, then load-test under realistic peak to prove it actually holds.

sections.s2_technical:
When database CPU hits 100 percent, resist the urge to scale up immediately. Scaling up hides the real cause and costs money forever. Start by measuring where the CPU goes.

Identify the top CPU-consuming queries. In PostgreSQL, `pg_stat_statements` ranks queries by `total_exec_time` and `calls`. On managed databases, Performance Insights shows the same. The query consuming the most total time is your first target, whether that is because it is individually slow or because it is called a huge number of times.

For each top query, find out why it is expensive. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and look for a sequential scan on a large table, which means a missing index — the CPU is burning cycles reading every row. Look for inefficient joins such as a nested loop over millions of rows where a hash join would be far cheaper; this usually means a missing index on the join key. Look for sorts spilling to disk.

Look at call frequency, not just per-call cost. A query that takes two milliseconds but runs fifty thousand times per second from an N+1 ORM pattern consumes more total CPU than one slow query. N+1 happens when loading a list of accounts and then firing one extra query per account for its transactions. The fix is a join fetch or batch fetch so one query replaces fifty-one.

Check connection-pool misconfiguration. A pool sized far larger than the database can handle lets too many heavy queries run concurrently, and context switching plus contention drives CPU up. Sometimes a smaller, well-sized pool actually reduces CPU because it limits concurrency to what the database can efficiently handle.

Apply the fix: add the missing index, rewrite the inefficient join, fix the N+1 with a fetch join or batch size, add caching for hot read-mostly queries, and right-size the pool.

Finally, load-test under realistic traffic. This step is non-negotiable because a fix that helps a single query in isolation can behave very differently under concurrency. A new index speeds reads but adds write cost; under a write-heavy peak that trade-off might hurt. Caching helps only if the hit rate is high under real access patterns. A load test with production-like concurrency, data volume, and query mix is the only honest proof that CPU stays healthy at peak. You replay captured traffic or use a tool like k6 or JMeter, watch CPU and P99 latency, and confirm headroom before declaring victory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — On salary day at the National Bank of India, the database CPU pins at 100 percent and every page slows. This is exactly how CPU saturation behaves — demand exceeds what the current queries can serve efficiently.

Problem 2 — The account dashboard loads a customer's accounts and then, for each account, fires a separate query for its recent transactions. With thousands of customers at peak, this becomes tens of thousands of tiny queries. This is exactly how an N+1 problem drives CPU — many cheap queries add up to enormous total cost.

Problem 3 — After fixing the N+1 with a join fetch, the team declares success on a single-user test. This is exactly why that is premature — only a realistic load test reveals whether CPU stays healthy under the real salary-day crowd.

We will build an `AccountDashboardService` showing the N+1 version and the fixed fetch-join version, a repository with a `@Query` using a join fetch, and a load-test script with k6 that drives realistic concurrency so we can confirm CPU headroom after the fix.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: salary-day peak traffic, thousands of dashboard requests, each summing transactions across many accounts.

Step 1: Investigation begins. We query `pg_stat_statements` and see that the single highest total-time entry is a tiny transactions-by-account query called fifty thousand times per second. The data tells us the cost is from frequency, not per-call slowness — a classic N+1.

Step 2: We confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the per-call query is fine individually but that there is no index on the join key, so each call does extra work. We add `idx_txn_account`.

Step 3: We change the repository to `findAllWithTransactions`, which issues one join-fetch query instead of one-plus-N. In the data path, fifty-one queries collapse into one.

Step 4: The service sums all transactions from the single result set. Total CPU for this endpoint drops sharply because the database runs one efficient join instead of tens of thousands of tiny lookups.

Step 5: The mandatory load test runs. We drive two hundred concurrent virtual users for two minutes with k6. The data here is realistic concurrency, not a single request. We watch database CPU and P95 latency.

Step 6: CPU now peaks around sixty percent with P95 under three hundred milliseconds, giving headroom. Only now do we declare the fix successful, because it held under realistic traffic rather than for one isolated query.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:30 INFO  AccountDashboardService - Summed 5000 accounts with a single fetch-join query
k6: http_req_duration p(95)=214ms  checks=100%  db_cpu_peak=61%
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When database CPU hits one hundred percent at peak, my first move is never to scale up the machine, because that hides the real cause and costs money forever. I start by identifying the top CPU-consuming queries using pg_stat_statements or Performance Insights, ranked by total execution time and by call count, because the biggest offender is often not one slow query but a cheap query called tens of thousands of times.

For each top query I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to understand why it is expensive. A sequential scan on a large table means a missing index. A nested loop over millions of rows means a missing index on a join key where a hash join would be far cheaper. A tiny query with a massive call count almost always means an N+1 pattern from the ORM, where loading a list then triggers one extra query per element. I also check the connection pool, because a pool sized far larger than the database can handle lets too many heavy queries run at once and actually raises CPU through contention.

I then apply the targeted fix: add the missing index, rewrite the inefficient join, replace N+1 with a fetch join or batch fetch so fifty-one queries become one, cache hot read-mostly results, and right-size the pool to the database's capacity rather than making it arbitrarily large.

The step I never skip is load testing under realistic traffic after the fix, and I always explain why: a change that looks great on a single query in isolation can behave completely differently under concurrency. A new index speeds reads but adds write cost, which can hurt during a write-heavy peak, and caching only helps if the hit rate is high under real access patterns. At the National Bank of India our salary-day dashboard pinned the database at one hundred percent because each request fired one query per account in an N+1 loop. I added an index on the join key and switched to a single fetch-join query, then I replayed salary-day concurrency with k6 at two hundred virtual users. CPU dropped to around sixty percent with P95 latency under three hundred milliseconds, and only then did I call it fixed — because the load test, not a single quiet query, is the honest proof that it holds under the real crowd.

answers.question: Why does `LIMIT ... OFFSET` pagination get slower on deep pages (the DB scans and discards all preceding rows — O(n) per page), and how does keyset/cursor pagination (`WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`) stay O(log n) at any depth?
answers.shortTitle: Why LIMIT/OFFSET pagination gets slower on deep pages, and keyset pagination

s1_definition.profdef: Offset-based pagination (`LIMIT n OFFSET m`) forces the database to read and discard all `m` preceding rows before returning the page, so cost grows linearly with page depth — O(m). Keyset (cursor) pagination replaces the offset with a `WHERE` condition on the last-seen sorted key (`WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`), letting an index seek jump directly to the start of the page, so cost stays O(log n) at any depth.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants page five hundred of his transaction history. With OFFSET, the clerk counts past the first ten thousand transactions one by one and throws them away just to hand over the next ten — exhausting on deep pages. With keyset pagination, Rajesh says "continue from the last transaction I saw," and the clerk uses the index to jump straight there, which is just as fast on page five hundred as on page one.
s1_definition.oneliner: OFFSET re-reads everything before the page (slower the deeper you go); keyset seeks straight to the page using the last-seen key (fast at any depth).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Offset-based pagination (`LIMIT n OFFSET m`) forces the database to read and discard all `m` preceding rows before returning the page, so cost grows linearly with page depth — O(m). Keyset (cursor) pagination replaces the offset with a `WHERE` condition on the last-seen sorted key (`WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`), letting an index seek jump directly to the start of the page, so cost stays O(log n) at any depth.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants page five hundred of his transaction history. With OFFSET, the clerk counts past the first ten thousand transactions one by one and throws them away just to hand over the next ten — exhausting on deep pages. With keyset pagination, Rajesh says "continue from the last transaction I saw," and the clerk uses the index to jump straight there, which is just as fast on page five hundred as on page one.

**One line to remember:** OFFSET re-reads everything before the page (slower the deeper you go); keyset seeks straight to the page using the last-seen key (fast at any depth).

sections.s2_technical:
With offset pagination, a query like `SELECT * FROM transactions ORDER BY txn_id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10000` cannot magically start at row ten thousand. The database must produce the sorted stream, count through the first ten thousand rows, discard every one of them, and only then emit the next ten. The discarded work is pure waste, and it grows with the offset. Page one discards zero rows; page one thousand discards ten thousand rows every single time it is requested. That is why deep pages crawl — it is O(offset) work per page.

Keyset pagination removes the offset entirely. Instead of asking for "skip ten thousand," you remember the sort key of the last row shown — say the last `txn_id` was 10000 — and the next page is `SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE txn_id > 10000 ORDER BY txn_id LIMIT 10`. If `txn_id` is indexed, the database performs an index seek directly to the entry just after 10000 and reads ten rows. It never touches the preceding ten thousand. Because an index seek is a B-tree descent, the cost is O(log n) to locate the start plus O(n) to read the page, and crucially it is identical whether you are on page one or page one million.

The trade-off is that keyset pagination gives you "next page" and "previous page" navigation rather than arbitrary "jump to page 500." For infinite-scroll feeds, transaction histories, and APIs, that is exactly what you want. For a true random-access page picker you need a stable sort and a composite cursor.

The cursor must be on a unique, ordered column, or a composite of columns that together are unique, otherwise rows with equal keys can be skipped or duplicated across pages. A common pattern is ordering by a timestamp plus the primary key as a tiebreaker: `WHERE (created_at, id) > (:last_ts, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT n`, which requires a composite index on `(created_at, id)`.

Keyset also plays well with stable results under concurrent inserts. With OFFSET, inserting rows while a user paginates shifts everything and causes duplicates or skips. With keyset, you are anchored to a real key, so new rows inserted after your cursor simply appear on later pages naturally.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, Rajesh scrolls his years-long transaction history. The first few pages load instantly, but by the time he reaches older transactions the app stalls for seconds. This is exactly how OFFSET pagination behaves — each deep page re-reads and discards everything before it.

Problem 2 — While Rajesh scrolls, new transactions keep posting to his account. With OFFSET, the same transaction sometimes appears twice or a transaction is skipped as rows shift. This is exactly how OFFSET loses stability under concurrent inserts.

Problem 3 — We switch to "load more from where you left off." This is exactly how keyset pagination works — anchor on the last-seen key and seek forward.

We will build a `TransactionHistoryService` with both an offset method (to show the problem) and a keyset method using `(txnDate, txnId)` as the cursor, backed by a composite index, so deep pages stay fast.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__keyset_index.sql
-- Composite index matching the keyset order: (account_id, txn_date, txn_id)
-- Enables an index seek directly to the cursor position at any depth.
CREATE INDEX idx_hist_keyset ON transactions(account_id, txn_date, txn_id);

-- SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001'
--   ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10000;   -- O(offset)

-- FAST: keyset seeks straight to the row after the cursor
-- SELECT * FROM transactions
--   WHERE account_id='SAV2001'
--     AND (txn_date, txn_id) > ('2024-03-01', 55123)
--   ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id LIMIT 10;                -- O(log n)
```

```bash
# KEYSET (index seek, constant work at any depth):
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001' \
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's `SAV2001` history, page size ten, requesting a deep page.

Step 1: First page. The client has no cursor, so the service calls `firstPage` with limit ten. The index seeks to the start of Rajesh's transactions and reads ten rows. The last row's `(txnDate, txnId)` becomes the cursor the client stores.

Step 2: Next page. The client sends back the cursor, say `('2024-03-01', 55123)`. The service calls `nextPage`. The query condition `(txn_date, txn_id) > ('2024-03-01', 55123)` lets the composite index seek directly to the row after the cursor.

Step 3: Deep page. Even on the five-hundredth page, the cursor still points to a real key, so the index seek jumps straight there and reads ten rows. No preceding rows are read or discarded. The work is identical to page two.

Step 4: Contrast with OFFSET. Had we used `OFFSET 10000`, the database would produce the sorted stream and discard ten thousand rows before returning ten — wasted work that grows with depth.

Step 5: Under concurrent inserts, new transactions post while Rajesh scrolls. Because keyset is anchored to a real key, those new rows naturally appear on later pages without duplicating or skipping anything.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:40 INFO  TransactionHistoryService - First page for SAV2001 (10 rows)
2026-10-25 13:50:41 INFO  TransactionHistoryService - Next page for SAV2001 after (2024-03-01, 55123) — seek, not scan
```

```
    page 1000: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 9990 → read+discard 9990 +10 O(offset)  ✗ slow

    page 1:  firstPage LIMIT 10                                   → index seek
    cursor = (2024-03-01, 55123)
    page N:  WHERE (txn_date,txn_id) > (2024-03-01,55123) LIMIT 10
             │ idx_hist_keyset seeks straight to row after cursor  O(log n)  ✓ fast
    ▼
  Same latency on page 1 and page 1,000,000
```

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Cursor/Iterator: PageCursor carries the last-seen key   │
  │   WHY: stateless server, stable results under inserts   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  TransactionHistoryService    │ uses   │   PageCursor         │
  │ ───────────────────────────── │───────▶│ - lastTxnDate: Date  │
  │ - repo: TransactionRepository │        │ - lastTxnId: long    │
  │ + page(acct, cursor, size)    │        └──────────────────────┘
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ uses
                  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> TransactionRepository    │
  │  + firstPage(acct, limit): List          │
  │  + nextPage(acct, lastDate, lastId, lim) │ ← (date,id) > cursor, index seek
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for nextPage():
    Pre:  cursor = last row's (txnDate, txnId); composite index exists
    Post: returns up to `size` rows strictly after the cursor, sorted
    Perf: O(log n) seek regardless of page depth
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Offset pagination gets slower on deep pages because the database cannot magically start at row ten thousand. For LIMIT ten OFFSET ten thousand, it must produce the sorted stream, count through and discard all ten thousand preceding rows, and only then return the next ten. That discarded work is pure waste and it grows with the offset, so page one is instant but page one thousand crawls — it is order-of-offset work every time the page is requested. Offset also loses stability under concurrent inserts, because new rows shift the window and cause duplicates or skips.

Keyset, or cursor, pagination fixes this by removing the offset entirely. Instead of skipping rows, I remember the sort key of the last row shown and ask for everything after it: WHERE the sort key is greater than the last-seen key, ORDER BY that key, LIMIT n. If the sort key is indexed, the database performs an index seek directly to the row after the cursor and reads only the page. The cost is a B-tree descent plus the page read, which is order log n, and it is identical whether you are on page one or page one million.

The one requirement is that the cursor must be on a unique ordered column, or a composite of columns that are unique together, backed by a matching composite index. A very common banking pattern is ordering by a timestamp with the primary key as a tiebreaker, using a row-value comparison on the pair and a composite index on that pair. The trade-off is that keyset gives natural next-page and previous-page navigation rather than arbitrary jump-to-page-500, which is exactly right for transaction histories, feeds, and APIs.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's multi-year transaction history loaded instantly on the first pages but stalled for seconds once he scrolled deep, and transactions sometimes appeared twice because new ones kept posting while he scrolled. I replaced offset pagination with keyset pagination anchored on the transaction date and id pair, backed by a composite index on account, date, and id. Deep pages became as fast as the first page because the index seeks straight to the cursor, and the duplicates disappeared because the cursor is anchored to a real key. The sentence I always remember is that offset re-reads everything before the page while keyset seeks straight to it, so keyset stays fast at any depth.

answers.question: What is the difference between OLTP (row-oriented stores like PostgreSQL — fast single-row transactions) and OLAP (columnar stores like Redshift/BigQuery — fast aggregations over few columns), and why should you NOT run heavy analytics on your production OLTP database?
answers.shortTitle: OLTP versus OLAP, and why not to run analytics on your OLTP database

s1_definition.profdef: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems like PostgreSQL and MySQL are row-oriented stores optimized for many small, concurrent read/write transactions touching few rows each, with strong consistency and low latency. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) systems like Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake are column-oriented stores optimized for scanning and aggregating a few columns across billions of rows. Running heavy analytics on a production OLTP database competes for the same CPU, memory, buffer cache, and locks that serve live customer transactions, degrading both.
s1_definition.analogy: OLTP is the busy teller counter at the National Bank — thousands of quick deposits and withdrawals, each touching one account, needing to be fast and correct. OLAP is the analyst in the back room who asks "what was the total deposit volume across all branches for the last five years?" If you force the teller counter to also run that giant report, the queue freezes while the machine chews through billions of rows. You keep the two jobs on separate systems.
s1_definition.oneliner: OLTP serves fast single-row transactions; OLAP scans few columns across billions of rows — keep heavy analytics off your transactional database.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems like PostgreSQL and MySQL are row-oriented stores optimized for many small, concurrent read/write transactions touching few rows each, with strong consistency and low latency. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) systems like Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake are column-oriented stores optimized for scanning and aggregating a few columns across billions of rows. Running heavy analytics on a production OLTP database competes for the same CPU, memory, buffer cache, and locks that serve live customer transactions, degrading both.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** OLTP is the busy teller counter at the National Bank — thousands of quick deposits and withdrawals, each touching one account, needing to be fast and correct. OLAP is the analyst in the back room who asks "what was the total deposit volume across all branches for the last five years?" If you force the teller counter to also run that giant report, the queue freezes while the machine chews through billions of rows. You keep the two jobs on separate systems.

**One line to remember:** OLTP serves fast single-row transactions; OLAP scans few columns across billions of rows — keep heavy analytics off your transactional database.

sections.s2_technical:
The core difference is physical storage layout. OLTP databases store data row by row: all columns of one account sit together on disk. This is perfect for a transaction like "read Rajesh's full account row, update his balance" because one small read or write touches one place. Indexes make finding that single row fast, and row locking keeps concurrent transactions correct.

OLAP databases store data column by column: all the `amount` values across millions of rows sit together, all the `txn_date` values sit together, and so on. This is perfect for "sum the amount column across five years" because the engine reads only the `amount` column — not the fifty other columns in each row — and compresses it heavily since similar values cluster. Columnar scans plus compression plus massive parallelism make aggregations over billions of rows fast.

Now consider why each is bad at the other's job. An OLAP columnar store is terrible at updating one account's balance, because a single logical row is scattered across many column files. An OLTP row store is terrible at summing one column across billions of rows, because it must read every full row, dragging in all the columns you did not want, and it has no columnar compression to help.

The reason you must not run heavy analytics on your production OLTP database is resource contention. That five-year aggregation will read a huge fraction of the table, evicting the hot pages that live transactions depend on from the buffer cache, so afterwards even fast transactions hit disk. It consumes CPU and memory that the teller traffic needs. It can hold shared locks or generate long-running snapshots that bloat the database. The result is exactly the connection-pool and latency cascade where one heavy query slows everything.

The standard architecture separates the two. Writes and live reads go to the OLTP primary. Data is then replicated or ETL'd into an OLAP warehouse — through change-data-capture, nightly batch loads, or streaming pipelines — where analysts run their heavy queries without touching production. A lighter middle ground is a read replica of the OLTP database for moderate reporting, but true heavy analytics belong in a columnar warehouse. This separation also lets each system scale independently and use the storage format suited to its workload.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the live transfer system runs on PostgreSQL and serves thousands of small transfers per second. This is exactly what OLTP is for — fast, correct, single-account transactions.

Problem 2 — The finance team starts running a "total deposits by month across five years" report directly against PostgreSQL during business hours, and the teller app slows to a crawl. This is exactly why you do not run analytics on OLTP — the report scans the whole table, evicts hot pages, and starves live traffic.

Problem 3 — We move the heavy aggregation into a columnar warehouse fed by change-data-capture, so analysts query there while PostgreSQL stays fast for customers. This is exactly the OLTP/OLAP separation.

We will build a `TransferService` for the OLTP path and an `AnalyticsService` that queries the warehouse (represented by a separate datasource), plus a CDC-style exporter concept, so the two workloads never compete.

```
│   └── src/main/java/com/bank/oltp/

    └── olap-application.yml
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- OLTP (PostgreSQL) — row store, fast single-row writes
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

-- OLAP (Redshift/BigQuery) — columnar, fast aggregation.
-- In Redshift you choose column encodings and a sort/dist key.
CREATE TABLE fact_transactions (
    txn_date   DATE,
    account_id VARCHAR(20),
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2),
    txn_type   VARCHAR(10)
)
DISTSTYLE KEY DISTKEY (account_id)
SORTKEY (txn_date);

-- Heavy aggregation that belongs on OLAP, NOT on the OLTP primary:
-- SELECT date_trunc('month', txn_date) AS m, SUM(amount)
-- FROM fact_transactions WHERE txn_type='DEPOSIT'
-- GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://oltp-primary:5432/bankdb
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
---
# olap-application.yml — analytics warehouse (separate system)
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:redshift://warehouse.cluster:5439/analytics
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 5   # few, long-running analytical queries
```

```bash

mvn -pl oltp-service clean package
java -jar oltp-service/target/oltp-service.jar --spring.config.location=resources/oltp-application.yml

# Analytics service (warehouse) — separate deployment, separate datasource
mvn -pl analytics-service clean package
java -jar analytics-service/target/analytics-service.jar --spring.config.location=resources/olap-application.yml

# Data pipeline: CDC from PostgreSQL → warehouse (e.g. Debezium → Kafka → loader)
# Analysts query the warehouse; the OLTP primary stays fast for customers.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: thousands of live transfers per second plus one five-year deposit report.

Step 1: A transfer arrives. `TransferService` runs two tiny single-row updates on the PostgreSQL primary. Because PostgreSQL stores each account as a contiguous row, the update touches one small place and commits in milliseconds.

Step 2: Change-data-capture reads the write-ahead log of these committed changes and streams them into a pipeline. The live database is not queried by analytics at all.

Step 3: The pipeline loads the changes into the columnar warehouse's `fact_transactions` table. Here the `amount`, `txn_date`, and `txn_type` columns are stored separately and compressed.

Step 4: The finance team runs the monthly deposit aggregation via `AnalyticsService`, which points at the warehouse. The columnar engine reads only the `amount`, `txn_date`, and `txn_type` columns across billions of rows, in parallel, and returns monthly totals.

Step 5: Throughout the heavy report, the OLTP primary's buffer cache stays warm with live account pages, so teller transactions remain fast. The two workloads never compete because they live on separate systems with storage layouts suited to each.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:50 INFO  TransferService - OLTP transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001
2026-10-25 13:50:51 INFO  AnalyticsService - Running 5-year deposit aggregation on the OLAP warehouse
```

```
  LIVE TRAFFIC (OLTP)                         ANALYTICS (OLAP)
  ┌──────────────┐                            ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Teller / App │                            │ Finance analysts  │
  └──────┬───────┘                            └─────────┬─────────┘
         │ small single-row txns                        │ heavy aggregations
         ▼                                              ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐   CDC (WAL) → Kafka   ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ PostgreSQL (row) │══════════════════════▶│ Redshift/BigQuery      │
  │ accounts         │   nightly/stream load │ fact_transactions      │
  │ fast writes      │                       │ columnar + compressed  │
  └──────────────────┘                       │ scans FEW columns      │
   buffer cache stays warm                   │ over BILLIONS of rows  │
   for live transactions                     └───────────────────────┘

  ✗ Do NOT run the 5-year SUM on PostgreSQL — it evicts hot pages,
    burns CPU, and freezes the teller queue.
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Two Services, Two Stores ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ──────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: TransferService = writes; AnalyticsService = reads   │
  │ D: each depends on its OWN datasource abstraction       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │       TransferService         │   │       AnalyticsService         │
  │ - oltp: JdbcTemplate (PG)     │   │ - olap: JdbcTemplate (Redshift)│
  │ @Transactional                │   │ (read-only, long queries)      │
  │ + transfer(from,to,amount)    │   │ + monthlyDepositTotals(): List │
  │   single-row UPDATEs          │   │   SUM over few columns         │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

  Storage layout:
    OLTP row:  [SAV2001 | Rajesh | 1,000,000 | ACTIVE]  ← one read = one txn
    OLAP col:  amount:   [50000, 25000, 70000, ...]     ← scan one column
               txn_date: [2024-03-01, 2024-03-01, ...]  ← compressed

  Contract:
    OLTP: fast single-row, strong consistency, low latency
    OLAP: fast aggregation over billions, eventually-consistent copy
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
OLTP and OLAP differ fundamentally in how they store data on disk. OLTP databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL are row-oriented: all the columns of one account sit together, which is perfect for a transaction that reads or updates a single account's row quickly and correctly under heavy concurrency. OLAP databases like Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake are column-oriented: all the values of one column sit together and are heavily compressed, which is perfect for scanning and aggregating a few columns across billions of rows.

Each is deliberately bad at the other's job. A columnar store is poor at updating one account's balance because a single logical row is scattered across many column files. A row store is poor at summing one column across billions of rows because it must read every full row, dragging in all the columns you did not ask for, with no columnar compression to help.

You must not run heavy analytics on your production OLTP database because of resource contention. A five-year aggregation reads a huge fraction of the table, evicts the hot pages that live transactions depend on from the buffer cache, burns the CPU and memory the live traffic needs, and can hold long-running snapshots that bloat the database. The result is that your fast customer transactions suddenly hit disk and the whole system slows — one heavy query dragging everything down. The correct architecture keeps writes and live reads on the OLTP primary and replicates or ETLs the data into a columnar warehouse through change-data-capture or batch pipelines, where analysts run their heavy queries without ever touching production.

At the National Bank of India, the finance team began running a five-year monthly deposit report directly against our PostgreSQL primary during business hours, and the teller application slowed to a crawl because the report scanned the whole table and evicted the live account pages from cache. I moved that workload into a columnar warehouse fed by change-data-capture, so analysts query the warehouse while PostgreSQL stays fast for customers. The line I always keep in mind is that OLTP serves fast single-row transactions and OLAP scans few columns over billions of rows, so I keep heavy analytics off the transactional database.

answers.question: What is Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) — changes are appended to a log and fsync'd BEFORE the data pages are updated, giving durability (replay the log on crash) and enabling point-in-time recovery and replication — and how does it shape a ledger database's backup strategy (a base backup + archived WAL segments lets you restore to any moment)?
answers.shortTitle: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and how it shapes a ledger backup strategy

s1_definition.profdef: Write-Ahead Logging is a durability protocol where every change is first appended to a sequential log and flushed to disk (fsync) BEFORE the corresponding data pages are modified. Because the log records the intended change durably first, a crash can be recovered by replaying the log. The same stream of WAL records enables physical replication to replicas and point-in-time recovery when combined with a base backup and archived WAL segments.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, before a clerk changes any balance in the big ledger, he first writes the exact instruction — "debit SAV2001 by 50,000" — into a sequential diary and makes sure the ink is dry (fsync). Only then does he update the ledger page. If the power fails mid-update, the bank reopens the diary and re-applies every instruction that was written down, so no committed transaction is ever lost, and the ledger is reconstructed exactly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Log the change durably first, update the data pages after — so a crash is recovered by replaying the log, and archived logs plus a base backup let you restore to any moment.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Write-Ahead Logging is a durability protocol where every change is first appended to a sequential log and flushed to disk (fsync) BEFORE the corresponding data pages are modified. Because the log records the intended change durably first, a crash can be recovered by replaying the log. The same stream of WAL records enables physical replication to replicas and point-in-time recovery when combined with a base backup and archived WAL segments.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, before a clerk changes any balance in the big ledger, he first writes the exact instruction — "debit SAV2001 by 50,000" — into a sequential diary and makes sure the ink is dry (fsync). Only then does he update the ledger page. If the power fails mid-update, the bank reopens the diary and re-applies every instruction that was written down, so no committed transaction is ever lost, and the ledger is reconstructed exactly.

**One line to remember:** Log the change durably first, update the data pages after — so a crash is recovered by replaying the log, and archived logs plus a base backup let you restore to any moment.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem WAL solves is the gap between "the transaction said COMMIT" and "the data pages are safely on disk." Writing the actual data pages randomly across disk on every commit would be slow, and a crash in the middle would corrupt the database. WAL decouples durability from the physical page writes.

When a transaction commits, PostgreSQL appends compact records describing the change to the WAL — a sequential file — and calls fsync so those records are physically on disk before it reports success. Sequential appends are fast. The actual data pages in the buffer cache are flushed to their random locations later, in the background, by the checkpointer. This is the "write-ahead" guarantee: the log is ahead of the data.

Durability on crash: if the server dies, on restart it reads the WAL from the last checkpoint forward and replays every committed change against the data files, redoing anything that had not yet been flushed. Any transaction that had committed is recovered; any that had not is discarded. This is crash recovery, and it is why a committed transfer is never lost.

Replication: a replica is just another server replaying the same WAL stream. The primary ships WAL records to replicas, which apply them to stay in sync. Streaming replication sends WAL continuously; this is how read replicas and standbys work.

Point-in-time recovery (PITR): this is the heart of a ledger backup strategy. You take a base backup — a full physical copy of the data directory — at some moment, then continuously archive every WAL segment the database fills. To recover, you restore the base backup and replay archived WAL up to any chosen timestamp or transaction. That means you can restore to "9:59:59 AM, one second before the bad batch job ran," not just to last night's snapshot.

For a ledger database this is decisive. A ledger must be auditable and must never lose a committed entry. The backup strategy is therefore: a periodic base backup plus continuous WAL archiving to durable storage like S3. This gives a recovery point objective of essentially zero committed-data loss, because every committed transaction is in an archived WAL segment, and it gives surgical recovery to any moment, which is exactly what you need to undo a faulty migration or a corrupting job without losing the good transactions that followed earlier.

Operational notes: checkpoints bound how much WAL must be replayed on recovery; more frequent checkpoints mean faster recovery but more write amplification. WAL archiving must itself be durable and monitored, because a gap in archived segments breaks the recovery chain. You periodically test restores, because an untested backup is a hope, not a strategy.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a transfer commits and the system reports success, but the server loses power one second later before the data pages are flushed. This is exactly what WAL protects against — on restart, the committed transfer is replayed from the log and is not lost.

Problem 2 — A faulty end-of-day batch at 10:00 AM corrupts thousands of balances. Last night's snapshot would lose a whole day of real transactions. This is exactly where point-in-time recovery helps — restore the base backup and replay WAL up to 9:59:59 AM.

Problem 3 — The ledger must prove no committed entry was ever lost for audit. This is exactly why continuous WAL archiving matters — every committed transaction lives in an archived segment.

We will build a `LedgerService` whose transfers commit durably, and a conceptual `RecoveryRunbook` plus the archive and PITR configuration, showing base-backup-plus-WAL as the ledger's backup strategy.

```
ledger-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/ledger/

│   │   │   ├── service/

│   │   │   └── model/

│   │   └── resources/
```
