answers.question: Given an `orders(id, order_date, total_amount)` table, write a query to calculate revenue for each month (group by year and month).
answers.shortTitle: Monthly Revenue Report — GROUP BY Year and Month

s1_definition.profdef: A monthly revenue report groups every order row by the calendar year and month extracted from `order_date`, then sums `total_amount` within each group. You extract the year/month with functions like `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)` and `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)` (or `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`), put those in both the `SELECT` and the `GROUP BY`, aggregate with `SUM(total_amount)`, and order chronologically.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a shoebox full of order slips, each with a date and an amount. Rajesh the accountant wants to know how much money came in each month. He sorts the slips into monthly piles — all of January 2026 together, all of February 2026 together — and adds up the amounts in each pile. That sorting into month piles is `GROUP BY year, month`, and adding each pile is `SUM(total_amount)`.
s1_definition.oneliner: Extract year and month from the date, `GROUP BY` both, `SUM` the amount, and `ORDER BY` year, month for a chronological revenue report.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A monthly revenue report groups every order row by the calendar year and month extracted from `order_date`, then sums `total_amount` within each group. You extract the year/month with functions like `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)` and `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)` (or `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`), put those in both the `SELECT` and the `GROUP BY`, aggregate with `SUM(total_amount)`, and order chronologically.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a shoebox full of order slips, each with a date and an amount. Rajesh the accountant wants to know how much money came in each month. He sorts the slips into monthly piles — all of January 2026 together, all of February 2026 together — and adds up the amounts in each pile. That sorting into month piles is `GROUP BY year, month`, and adding each pile is `SUM(total_amount)`.

**One line to remember:** Extract year and month from the date, `GROUP BY` both, `SUM` the amount, and `ORDER BY` year, month for a chronological revenue report.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that `GROUP BY` collapses many rows that share the same key into one output row, and an aggregate function like `SUM` computes a single value per group. For a monthly report the grouping key is the pair (year, month), so two orders placed on different days of the same month land in the same group.

There are two common ways to express the key. The portable, standard way uses `EXTRACT`: `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)` returns the year as a number and `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)` returns 1 through 12. You select both, group by both, and sum the amount. For example in PostgreSQL:

```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)  AS yr,
       EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS mon,
       SUM(total_amount)              AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
ORDER BY yr, mon;
```

The second way uses `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`, which rounds every timestamp down to the first day of its month, so `2026-03-15` and `2026-03-28` both become `2026-03-01`. Grouping by that single truncated value is clean and keeps results sorted naturally as a date:

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month_start,
       SUM(total_amount)               AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
ORDER BY month_start;
```

A critical rule that trips juniors up: every non-aggregated column in the `SELECT` must appear in the `GROUP BY`. You cannot select `order_date` raw alongside `SUM` unless it is in the group key, because the engine would not know which of the many dates in the group to show. Grouping by year and month separately (rather than just month) matters because otherwise January 2025 and January 2026 would be merged into one "January" bucket, which is wrong for a multi-year report.

A senior nuance is performance and correctness. If `order_date` is a timestamp with time zone, truncation and extraction happen in the session time zone unless you convert explicitly, so a report "for IST" should convert with `order_date AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'` first. For large tables, an index on `order_date` helps range-limited reports (for example a single year), and in reporting warehouses you often pre-compute these monthly sums into a materialized view so the dashboard does not re-scan millions of rows every time. Also be aware `SUM` ignores `NULL` amounts, so if `total_amount` can be null you may want `SUM(COALESCE(total_amount, 0))` to treat missing as zero.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India runs a small merchant-orders platform where Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) place purchase orders funded from their accounts. The finance team needs a month-by-month revenue report to see seasonal trends and to reconcile against the general ledger. Right now someone exports a spreadsheet and manually sorts by month, which is slow and error-prone when orders span multiple years.

This is exactly what `GROUP BY year, month` with `SUM` solves — the database does the bucketing and totalling in one pass. Our mini-project builds a tiny in-memory version of the same SQL logic so you can see the grouping clearly: an `Order` record with a date and a `BigDecimal` amount, a repository holding the orders, and a `RevenueReportService` that groups orders by (year, month) and sums the amounts, mirroring the SQL exactly. The demo prints the monthly revenue for Rajesh's and Priya's orders across two years.

The code will contain: an `Order` class, an `OrderRepository` that returns all orders, a `MonthlyRevenue` result class holding year, month and total, a `RevenueReportService.monthlyRevenue()` method that performs the grouping and summing, and a `Demo` main method that loads sample orders and prints the report sorted by year then month.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five orders — two in January 2025 (12000 + 8000), one in February 2025 (15000), and two in January 2026 (20000 + 5000).

Step 1: The service calls `repo.findAll()`, which returns all five `Order` objects. In the real system this is the `orders` table being scanned or range-read by the `GROUP BY` query. The data lives as rows with a date and an amount.

Step 2: For each order, the service extracts the year and month from `orderDate` and builds a key like `"2025-01"`. This is the SQL `EXTRACT(YEAR ...)`/`EXTRACT(MONTH ...)` step — each row is tagged with which monthly bucket it belongs to. The amount stays unchanged; only the grouping tag is derived.

Step 3: The service merges each amount into a `TreeMap` keyed by that month string using `BigDecimal::add`. This is the `SUM(total_amount)` aggregation — the January 2025 bucket accumulates 12000 then 8000 to become 20000, while the February 2025 bucket holds 15000 and the January 2026 bucket accumulates 20000 then 5000 to become 25000.

Step 4: Because a `TreeMap` keeps keys in sorted order, iterating it yields `2025-01`, `2025-02`, `2026-01` in chronological order — the SQL `ORDER BY yr, mon`. Each entry is converted to a `MonthlyRevenue` object with year, month, and total.

Step 5: The application prints the three rows. The individual order amounts no longer appear; only the three monthly totals remain, which is the whole point of aggregation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To compute revenue per month I group the orders by the year and month taken from the order date and sum the total amount within each group. In standard SQL I write `SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS yr, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS mon, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) ORDER BY yr, mon`. On PostgreSQL I often prefer `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` as a single clean grouping key that also sorts naturally. The key rule is that every non-aggregated column I select must be in the GROUP BY, and I group by year and month together so that January of different years do not collapse into one bucket.

In our National Bank of India merchant platform the finance team needed a month-by-month revenue report across multiple years to spot seasonal trends and reconcile against the ledger. I replaced a manual spreadsheet sort with this grouped query, which the database does in a single pass. I also make sure that when the date is a timestamp with time zone I convert it to the bank's reporting zone like Asia/Kolkata before truncating, and that money is always summed as a decimal type so there is no floating-point rounding error. The line I remember is: extract year and month, group by both, sum the amount, and order chronologically.

answers.question: Given `Department` and `Employees` tables, write a query to find the number of employees in each department.
answers.shortTitle: Count Employees per Department — JOIN with GROUP BY

s1_definition.profdef: Counting employees per department joins the `Employees` table to the `Department` table on the department foreign key, groups the result by department, and applies `COUNT(*)` within each group. To include departments that currently have zero employees you use a `LEFT JOIN` from `Department` to `Employees` and `COUNT(e.id)` (counting the employee key, which skips NULLs) instead of `COUNT(*)`.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India head office, every employee carries a badge that says which department they belong to — Loans, Fraud, or Operations. Priya the HR manager wants a headcount per department. She lines up all the badges, sorts them into department piles, and counts each pile. Sorting into piles is `GROUP BY department`, and counting each pile is `COUNT(*)`. If the brand-new "Crypto Desk" has no staff yet, a LEFT JOIN still lists it with a count of zero.
s1_definition.oneliner: JOIN employees to departments, `GROUP BY` department, `COUNT(*)` the rows — and use `LEFT JOIN` with `COUNT(employee_id)` to show empty departments as zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting employees per department joins the `Employees` table to the `Department` table on the department foreign key, groups the result by department, and applies `COUNT(*)` within each group. To include departments that currently have zero employees you use a `LEFT JOIN` from `Department` to `Employees` and `COUNT(e.id)` (counting the employee key, which skips NULLs) instead of `COUNT(*)`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India head office, every employee carries a badge that says which department they belong to — Loans, Fraud, or Operations. Priya the HR manager wants a headcount per department. She lines up all the badges, sorts them into department piles, and counts each pile. Sorting into piles is `GROUP BY department`, and counting each pile is `COUNT(*)`. If the brand-new "Crypto Desk" has no staff yet, a LEFT JOIN still lists it with a count of zero.

**One line to remember:** JOIN employees to departments, `GROUP BY` department, `COUNT(*)` the rows — and use `LEFT JOIN` with `COUNT(employee_id)` to show empty departments as zero.

sections.s2_technical:
The task combines two operations: a join to bring department names next to employees, and a grouped count to tally per department. The simplest inner-join version counts only departments that have at least one employee:

```sql
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM department d
JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_name
ORDER BY employee_count DESC;
```

The `JOIN ... ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id` pairs each employee row with its department row. `GROUP BY d.dept_name` collapses all employees of the same department into one group, and `COUNT(*)` counts the rows in each group. I group by `d.dept_name` (and ideally `d.dept_id` too, since names could repeat) so the engine knows how to bucket.

The important subtlety is departments with no employees. An inner join drops any department that has no matching employee row, so a brand-new empty department would simply vanish from the report. To include it you flip to a `LEFT JOIN` starting from the department side, and you must count the employee column, not `*`:

```sql
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS employee_count
FROM department d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
ORDER BY employee_count DESC;
```

Here `COUNT(e.emp_id)` is deliberate: `COUNT(*)` would count the single NULL-filled row the LEFT JOIN manufactures for an empty department and wrongly report 1, whereas `COUNT(e.emp_id)` ignores NULLs and correctly reports 0. This is the classic COUNT-column-versus-COUNT-star distinction, and it is a favorite interview trap.

Another nuance is grouping by the id versus the name. Two different departments could theoretically share a display name, so grouping by the primary key `dept_id` is safer and then you also select `dept_name`. In standard SQL any selected non-aggregate must be in the GROUP BY; PostgreSQL relaxes this when you group by the primary key because the name is functionally dependent on it.

Senior-level points: an index on `employees(dept_id)` makes the join and grouping efficient on large tables. If you only want counts above a threshold, add `HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) > 10` — `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation, whereas `WHERE` filters rows before grouping. And if the question is "distinct managers per department" you would use `COUNT(DISTINCT e.manager_id)` rather than a plain count. The general skill being tested is understanding that a join defines the row set, `GROUP BY` defines the buckets, and the aggregate defines the number per bucket.
sections.s3_banking:

Priya in HR needs a live headcount per department for a staffing review: Loans has several officers, Fraud Analytics has a couple, and a newly created Crypto Desk has nobody yet. The current report uses an inner join and the empty Crypto Desk disappears entirely, which made leadership think the department did not exist — a real reporting bug.

Our mini-project models a `Department` and an `Employee`, a repository that holds both lists, and a `HeadcountService` that produces a count per department including empty ones by counting employees (not rows), mirroring the SQL `LEFT JOIN ... COUNT(e.emp_id)`.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To count employees per department I join the employees table to the department table on the department id, group by the department, and count. The subtle but important decision is whether empty departments must appear. If I only want departments that have staff I use an inner join and `COUNT(*)`: `SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(*) FROM department d JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_name`. If I must also show departments with zero employees I switch to a LEFT JOIN from department to employees and count the employee key rather than the row: `SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) FROM department d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name`. The reason `COUNT(e.emp_id)` matters is that a LEFT JOIN manufactures a NULL-filled row for an empty department, and `COUNT(*)` would wrongly report one while `COUNT(column)` ignores NULLs and correctly reports zero.

In our National Bank of India HR system a newly created Crypto Desk with no staff was disappearing from the headcount report because it used an inner join, which made leadership think the department did not exist. I fixed it with a LEFT JOIN and `COUNT(emp_id)` so the empty department shows a count of zero. The senior points I add are that I group by the department primary key rather than just the name to be safe when names could repeat, that I create an index on the employees' department column so the join and grouping stay fast on large tables, and that I use HAVING rather than WHERE when I need to filter on the aggregated count, for example departments with more than ten people. The line I remember is: join, group by department, and count the employee key with a LEFT JOIN so that empty departments show zero.

answers.question: Write a query to find the total amount of money spent by each customer.
answers.shortTitle: Total Money Spent by Each Customer — SUM with GROUP BY

s1_definition.profdef: Finding total spend per customer groups the orders (or payments) table by `customer_id` and applies `SUM(amount)` within each group. To also show the customer's name you join to the customers table, and to include customers who have never spent anything you use a `LEFT JOIN` from customers to orders with `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)` so a null total reads as zero.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, every customer has a stack of purchase receipts. Priya in finance wants to know each customer's lifetime spend. She gathers each customer's receipts into one pile per customer and adds up the amounts in that pile. Making one pile per customer is `GROUP BY customer_id`, and adding each pile is `SUM(amount)`. A customer who never bought anything has an empty pile — a LEFT JOIN still lists them with a total of zero.
s1_definition.oneliner: `GROUP BY customer_id` and `SUM(amount)` for total spend per customer — LEFT JOIN with `COALESCE(SUM,0)` to include non-spenders.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding total spend per customer groups the orders (or payments) table by `customer_id` and applies `SUM(amount)` within each group. To also show the customer's name you join to the customers table, and to include customers who have never spent anything you use a `LEFT JOIN` from customers to orders with `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)` so a null total reads as zero.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, every customer has a stack of purchase receipts. Priya in finance wants to know each customer's lifetime spend. She gathers each customer's receipts into one pile per customer and adds up the amounts in that pile. Making one pile per customer is `GROUP BY customer_id`, and adding each pile is `SUM(amount)`. A customer who never bought anything has an empty pile — a LEFT JOIN still lists them with a total of zero.

**One line to remember:** `GROUP BY customer_id` and `SUM(amount)` for total spend per customer — LEFT JOIN with `COALESCE(SUM,0)` to include non-spenders.

sections.s2_technical:
The essence is a grouped sum. If the amounts live in an `orders` table with a `customer_id`, the minimal query is:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
```

`GROUP BY customer_id` makes one group per customer, and `SUM(total_amount)` adds every order amount in that group. Ordering by the total descending gives a "biggest spenders first" ranking, which is what most business reports want.

Usually you also want the customer's name, which lives in a separate `customers` table, so you join:

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
```

With an inner join, a customer who has placed zero orders simply does not appear. If the report must list everyone, including newly onboarded customers who have not spent yet, switch to a LEFT JOIN and wrap the sum in `COALESCE` so the null becomes zero:

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
```

The reason `COALESCE` matters is that `SUM` over no rows returns `NULL`, not `0`. For a spend report, showing a blank is confusing, so `COALESCE(SUM(...), 0)` makes it read as a clean zero.

Several nuances are worth stating at senior level. First, `SUM` silently ignores `NULL` amounts, so if some order amounts can be null and you want them treated as zero, use `SUM(COALESCE(total_amount, 0))`. Second, money should be a `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC` type, never float, so the sum does not accumulate rounding error — this is non-negotiable in banking. Third, if a customer can have orders in multiple currencies you cannot blindly sum; you either filter to one currency or convert first, otherwise the total is meaningless. Fourth, for performance an index on `orders(customer_id)` supports the grouping, and for a very large orders table a pre-aggregated summary table or materialized view avoids rescanning history on every dashboard load. Finally, if you need "spend in the last 12 months" you add a `WHERE order_date >= ...` before grouping, remembering that `WHERE` filters rows and `HAVING` filters groups.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's loyalty team wants to reward high-spending customers with cashback tiers. They need each customer's total spend. Rajesh (SAV2001) has several orders, Priya (CUR3001) has one large order, and a newly onboarded customer has placed no orders yet but must still appear in the list (with zero) so the team can see the full customer base. An earlier version used an inner join and the new customer was missing, so the onboarding team could not confirm the account was live.

This is the LEFT-JOIN-plus-COALESCE-SUM pattern. Our mini-project models a `Customer` and an `Order`, a repository holding both, and a `SpendService` that totals each customer's spend including customers with no orders.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find the total money spent by each customer I group the orders by customer and sum the amount: `SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY total_spent DESC`. When I also need the customer name I join to the customers table and group by the customer id and name. The important decision is whether customers who have never spent must still appear. If they must, I use a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders and wrap the sum in COALESCE so an empty total reads as zero: `COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0)`, because SUM over no rows returns NULL, not zero, and a blank total is confusing on a report.

In our National Bank of India loyalty program we needed each customer's lifetime spend to assign cashback tiers, and a newly onboarded customer with no orders had to appear with zero so the onboarding team could confirm the account was live. The earlier inner-join version dropped that customer, which I fixed with the LEFT-JOIN-plus-COALESCE pattern. The line I remember is: group by customer, sum the amount, and LEFT JOIN with COALESCE to show non-spenders as zero.

answers.question: Write a query to find duplicate records in a table (GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT > 1).
answers.shortTitle: Find Duplicate Records — GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT > 1

s1_definition.profdef: To find duplicate records you group by the column or set of columns that defines "sameness," count the rows in each group, and keep only the groups whose count is greater than one using a `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` clause. `WHERE` cannot filter on an aggregate, so the count condition must go in `HAVING`, which filters groups after aggregation.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India KYC team suspects some customers registered twice with the same PAN. Priya takes every registration form, sorts them into piles by PAN number, and then only pulls out the piles that have two or more forms — those are the duplicates. Sorting into PAN piles is `GROUP BY pan`, counting each pile is `COUNT(*)`, and keeping only piles bigger than one is `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
s1_definition.oneliner: `GROUP BY` the columns that define a duplicate, then `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` — because you cannot filter an aggregate in `WHERE`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** To find duplicate records you group by the column or set of columns that defines "sameness," count the rows in each group, and keep only the groups whose count is greater than one using a `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` clause. `WHERE` cannot filter on an aggregate, so the count condition must go in `HAVING`, which filters groups after aggregation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India KYC team suspects some customers registered twice with the same PAN. Priya takes every registration form, sorts them into piles by PAN number, and then only pulls out the piles that have two or more forms — those are the duplicates. Sorting into PAN piles is `GROUP BY pan`, counting each pile is `COUNT(*)`, and keeping only piles bigger than one is `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.

**One line to remember:** `GROUP BY` the columns that define a duplicate, then `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` — because you cannot filter an aggregate in `WHERE`.

sections.s2_technical:
Duplicates are defined by which columns must match. If two rows with the same email are duplicates, you group by email. If a duplicate means the same first name, last name and date of birth, you group by all three. The pattern is:

```sql
SELECT pan, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM customers
GROUP BY pan
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY cnt DESC;
```

`GROUP BY pan` buckets rows by PAN, `COUNT(*)` tallies each bucket, and `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` discards buckets that appear only once, leaving only the PANs that repeat. The reason the count condition lives in `HAVING` and not `WHERE` is fundamental to SQL's order of evaluation: `WHERE` runs before grouping, on individual rows, so at that point the group count does not exist yet. `HAVING` runs after grouping, so it can see the aggregate. Writing `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` is a syntax error.

This query tells you which values are duplicated and how many times, but it returns one row per duplicated value, not the actual duplicate rows. If you need the full offending rows (to inspect or delete), you either join back or use a window function:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT c.*, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pan) AS pan_count
    FROM customers c
) t
WHERE pan_count > 1
ORDER BY pan;
```

Here `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pan)` annotates every row with how many rows share its PAN, without collapsing them, so you can filter to the full set of duplicate rows.

A few important nuances. First, if the duplicate key can contain `NULL`, remember two `NULL`s are not considered equal by `GROUP BY` in some engines and the behavior around NULL grouping differs, so define whether NULLs count as duplicates. Second, for case- or whitespace-insensitive duplicates (common with emails and names), you normalize inside the group key, for example `GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))`, otherwise `Rajesh@x.com` and `rajesh@x.com ` look distinct. Third, to actually remove duplicates you typically keep the lowest id and delete the rest, often with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY id)` and delete where the row number is greater than one. Fourth, finding duplicates after the fact is reactive; the durable fix is a `UNIQUE` constraint or unique index on the key so the database refuses to insert the second copy in the first place. For performance, an index on the grouped column makes the duplicate scan far cheaper.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India discovered that some customers exist twice in the `customers` table with the same PAN because the registration flow lacked a unique constraint and two near-simultaneous sign-ups both succeeded. Before adding the constraint, the data team must first find and clean the existing duplicates. Rajesh's PAN appears twice (two customer rows), Priya's PAN appears once. The team needs a report of every PAN that occurs more than once.

This is the classic `GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` pattern. Our mini-project models a `CustomerRow` with an id and a PAN, a repository holding rows including a duplicated PAN, and a `DuplicateFinderService` that returns the PANs occurring more than once, mirroring the SQL exactly.

The code will contain: a `CustomerRow` class, a `CustomerRepository`, a `DuplicateGroup` DTO (the key plus the count), a `DuplicateFinderService.findDuplicatePans()` method implementing group-count-having, and a `Demo` that prints the duplicated PANs.

Input data: three customer rows — two with PAN `ABCDE1234F` (Rajesh Kumar and Rajesh K) and one with PAN `PQRSX9876L` (Priya).

Step 1: The service reads all rows. In SQL this is the table scan the `GROUP BY` performs. Each row has an id, a name, and a PAN.

Step 2: For each row the service normalizes the PAN (trim and uppercase, mirroring `LOWER(TRIM(...))` normalization) and increments a counter keyed by that PAN. This is `COUNT(*)` grouped by PAN. After the pass, `ABCDE1234F` maps to 2 and `PQRSX9876L` maps to 1.

Step 3: The service keeps only groups whose count is greater than one. This is the `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` filter. `ABCDE1234F` survives with count 2; `PQRSX9876L` is discarded because it appears once.

Step 4: Results are sorted by count descending (`ORDER BY cnt DESC`). Only the duplicated PAN remains.

Step 5: The application prints the one duplicated PAN with its count. The data team now knows exactly which PAN to clean up before adding a unique constraint.

```
  7.   → return 1 DuplicateGroup
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicate records I group by the column or set of columns that defines a duplicate, count the rows in each group, and keep only the groups whose count exceeds one with a HAVING clause: `SELECT pan, COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY pan HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`. The reason the count condition must go in HAVING and not WHERE is SQL's evaluation order — WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, when the group count does not yet exist, whereas HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can see the count. If I need the actual duplicate rows rather than just the duplicated values, I use a window function, annotating each row with `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pan)` and filtering to rows where that is greater than one.

In our National Bank of India customer table we found some customers existed twice with the same PAN because the sign-up flow had no unique constraint and two near-simultaneous registrations both succeeded. I used this group-count-having query to list every duplicated PAN so the data team could clean them up, keeping the lowest id and deleting the rest with a ROW_NUMBER approach. The senior points I always add are that I normalize the key, for example with LOWER and TRIM on emails, so that case and whitespace variations are caught, that I must decide whether NULLs count as duplicates, and most importantly that finding duplicates is only the reactive half — the durable fix is a UNIQUE constraint or unique index on the key so the database itself refuses the second copy. The line I remember is: group by the duplicate key, then HAVING COUNT greater than one, and back it with a unique constraint so it never happens again.

answers.question: Given an `employee(ID, Name, Salary, City, Department)` table: find the max salary per city, the total salary per department, and the employee with the second-highest salary.
answers.shortTitle: Max Salary per City, Total Salary per Department, and Second-Highest Salary

s1_definition.profdef: These are three grouped/ranked queries. Max salary per city groups by city and applies `MAX(salary)`. Total salary per department groups by department and applies `SUM(salary)`. The second-highest salary is a ranking problem solved with `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)` filtered to rank 2, or with a subquery that finds the max salary below the overall max.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, HR has a sheet of every employee with salary, city, and department. First question: in each city, who earns the most — sort by city, pick the top salary in each city pile. Second question: what is each department's total salary cost — sort by department, add each department pile. Third question: who is the second-best paid overall — line everyone up by salary, the person just below the top is the answer.
s1_definition.oneliner: `MAX` grouped by city, `SUM` grouped by department, and `DENSE_RANK() = 2` (or a nested max-below-max subquery) for the second-highest salary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are three grouped/ranked queries. Max salary per city groups by city and applies `MAX(salary)`. Total salary per department groups by department and applies `SUM(salary)`. The second-highest salary is a ranking problem solved with `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)` filtered to rank 2, or with a subquery that finds the max salary below the overall max.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, HR has a sheet of every employee with salary, city, and department. First question: in each city, who earns the most — sort by city, pick the top salary in each city pile. Second question: what is each department's total salary cost — sort by department, add each department pile. Third question: who is the second-best paid overall — line everyone up by salary, the person just below the top is the answer.

**One line to remember:** `MAX` grouped by city, `SUM` grouped by department, and `DENSE_RANK() = 2` (or a nested max-below-max subquery) for the second-highest salary.

sections.s2_technical:
Part one, max salary per city, is a straightforward grouped aggregate:

```sql
SELECT city, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employee
GROUP BY city;
```

Each city becomes one group and `MAX(salary)` returns the largest salary in that city. If you also want the name of the person earning that max, a plain `GROUP BY` cannot give it (you cannot select `name` without aggregating it), so you use a window function: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY salary DESC)` and keep row 1 per city, which returns the full highest-paid employee row per city.

Part two, total salary per department, is another grouped aggregate:

```sql
SELECT department, SUM(salary) AS total_salary
FROM employee
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY total_salary DESC;
```

This gives the payroll cost per department, useful for budgeting.

Part three, the second-highest salary, is the interesting one because there are several correct approaches and each handles ties differently. The cleanest modern approach uses a window function:

```sql
SELECT name, salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employee
) t
WHERE rnk = 2;
```

`DENSE_RANK` assigns rank 1 to the highest salary, and every employee tied at the next distinct salary gets rank 2 — so if two people share the second-highest salary, both are returned, which is usually the desired behavior. If you instead wanted the second-highest distinct salary value only, `DENSE_RANK` is exactly right because it does not skip ranks on ties.

A classic subquery alternative without window functions finds the maximum salary that is strictly less than the overall maximum:

```sql
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee);
```

This returns just the value. It correctly handles duplicates of the top salary (because it looks for salaries strictly below the single max value), and returns `NULL` if there is no second distinct salary. A `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` approach like `ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` is tempting but wrong when the top salary is duplicated, because the second row might just be another person at the top salary, so I avoid it unless the salaries are guaranteed distinct.

Senior nuances: `DENSE_RANK` versus `RANK` matters — `RANK` skips numbers after ties (1,1,3) while `DENSE_RANK` does not (1,1,2), so for "second-highest distinct salary" `DENSE_RANK` is the safe choice. For per-department second-highest you add `PARTITION BY department` to the window. Money should be a decimal type. And for large tables an index on salary (or on the partition column plus salary) helps the ordering.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's compensation team needs three things from the employee roster: the top earner's salary in each city for market benchmarking, the total payroll cost per department for budgeting, and the second-highest salary overall for a pay-band review. Rajesh and Priya are among the staff spread across Mumbai and Delhi in the Loans and Fraud departments. A naive attempt used `LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` for the second-highest and returned the wrong person when two people shared the top salary.

This exercises `MAX` grouping, `SUM` grouping, and `DENSE_RANK`-based ranking. Our mini-project models an `Employee`, a repository, and a `CompensationService` with three methods mirroring the three queries.

The code will contain: an `Employee` class, an `EmployeeRepository`, a `CompensationService` with `maxSalaryPerCity()`, `totalSalaryPerDepartment()`, and `secondHighestSalary()`, and a `Demo` printing all three results.

Step 4: It sorts those distinct salaries descending: 150000, 120000, 110000. The element at index 1 (rank 2) is 120000 — the second-highest distinct salary. sections.s6_takeaway:
This question is really three. For the maximum salary per city I group by city and take MAX: `SELECT city, MAX(salary) FROM employee GROUP BY city`, and if I also need the person's name I use `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY salary DESC)` and keep row one. For the total salary per department I group by department and SUM: `SELECT department, SUM(salary) FROM employee GROUP BY department`. For the second-highest salary I prefer a window function, `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)` filtered to rank two, because DENSE_RANK does not skip ranks on ties so it correctly returns the second-highest distinct salary even when several people share the top salary. A pure-SQL alternative is `SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee)`.

In our National Bank of India compensation review we needed the top earner per city for benchmarking, the payroll cost per department for budgeting, and the second-highest salary for a pay-band study. A first attempt used `LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` for the second-highest and returned the wrong person because two employees shared the top salary, so the offset simply landed on another top earner. I switched to DENSE_RANK, which treats tied salaries as the same rank and gives the correct next distinct value. The senior points I add are that DENSE_RANK versus RANK matters because RANK skips numbers after ties, that for a per-department second-highest I add PARTITION BY department to the window, that salary is sensitive data so I gate access by role and audit it, and that money is always a decimal type. The line I remember is: MAX grouped by city, SUM grouped by department, and DENSE_RANK equal to two for the second-highest salary.

answers.question: Write a query to find the top 5 employees with salary greater than the average salary (LIMIT/TOP and RANK versions).
answers.shortTitle: Top 5 Employees Earning Above the Average Salary — LIMIT and RANK Versions

s1_definition.profdef: This filters employees whose salary exceeds the overall average (computed with a subquery `(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee)`), then takes the top five by salary. The `LIMIT`/`TOP` version orders by salary descending and caps the rows. The `RANK` version assigns a rank with a window function and keeps ranks one through five, which handles ties at the fifth position more predictably.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to reward its best-paid high performers. First find the average salary of everyone. Then keep only people earning more than that average. Then from those, take the top five. The "take top five" can be a simple cut-off of five rows, or a ranking where everyone tied at fifth place is also included — that choice is the LIMIT version versus the RANK version.
s1_definition.oneliner: Filter `salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) ...)`, then `ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5`, or use `RANK()`/`DENSE_RANK()` and keep ranks `<= 5` to handle ties.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This filters employees whose salary exceeds the overall average (computed with a subquery `(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee)`), then takes the top five by salary. The `LIMIT`/`TOP` version orders by salary descending and caps the rows. The `RANK` version assigns a rank with a window function and keeps ranks one through five, which handles ties at the fifth position more predictably.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to reward its best-paid high performers. First find the average salary of everyone. Then keep only people earning more than that average. Then from those, take the top five. The "take top five" can be a simple cut-off of five rows, or a ranking where everyone tied at fifth place is also included — that choice is the LIMIT version versus the RANK version.

**One line to remember:** Filter `salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) ...)`, then `ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5`, or use `RANK()`/`DENSE_RANK()` and keep ranks `<= 5` to handle ties.

sections.s2_technical:
The shared piece is the average comparison. The overall average must be computed as a scalar subquery because you cannot compare a row's salary to an aggregate of the whole table directly in `WHERE` without one:

```sql
SELECT name, salary
FROM employee
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee)
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 5;                      -- MySQL/PostgreSQL
-- SQL Server: SELECT TOP 5 ... ORDER BY salary DESC
```

The subquery `(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee)` runs once and returns a single number, the average. The outer query keeps only rows above it, sorts them highest first, and takes the first five. This is the `LIMIT`/`TOP` version and it is simple and fast, but it has a subtle behavior: if the fifth and sixth employees earn exactly the same salary, `LIMIT 5` arbitrarily includes one and excludes the other, which can feel unfair in a rewards context.

The `RANK` version addresses ties explicitly using a window function:

```sql
SELECT name, salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, salary,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employee
    WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee)
) t
WHERE rnk <= 5
ORDER BY rnk;
```

Here the filtering to above-average happens first, then `RANK()` numbers the survivors by salary descending, and `WHERE rnk <= 5` keeps the top five ranks. If three people tie for the top salary, `RANK` gives them all rank 1 and the next distinct salary gets rank 4 (RANK skips), so you could end up returning more than five rows when there are ties — which is often the intended "fair" behavior for a rewards program. If you want exactly five distinct salary tiers, you use `DENSE_RANK` instead. If you want precisely five rows regardless of ties and a deterministic tie-breaker, you add a secondary sort key like `ORDER BY salary DESC, id` and use `ROW_NUMBER()`.

The key senior distinctions are: `ROW_NUMBER` always gives exactly one row per position (good for strict pagination but arbitrary on ties), `RANK` gives tied rows the same number and then skips (1,1,3), and `DENSE_RANK` gives tied rows the same number without skipping (1,1,2). For "top 5," the LIMIT approach is fine when salaries are effectively unique or when arbitrary tie-breaking is acceptable; the RANK approach is better when you must treat ties fairly. Note also that `AVG` ignores NULL salaries, so if NULLs are possible you decide whether to coalesce them. For performance, an index on salary helps both the ordering and the average scan.
sections.s3_banking:

The HR system previously used a plain `LIMIT 5` and in one cycle two employees tied at the fifth-highest salary; one got a bonus and the other did not, purely because of row ordering, which triggered a fairness complaint. HR now wants the RANK-based version so ties at the boundary are handled consistently.

This exercises an average-comparison subquery plus both the LIMIT and RANK approaches. Our mini-project models an `Employee`, a repository, and a `BonusService` exposing both a `topFiveByLimit()` and a `topFiveByRank()` method so the difference is visible.

The code will contain: an `Employee` class, an `EmployeeRepository`, a `BonusService` with the two methods, and a `Demo` printing both results so the tie behavior is clear.

Input data: seven employees with salaries 120000, 150000, 110000, 140000, 130000, 130000, 50000.

Step 1: The service computes the average salary. The sum is 830000 over seven employees, giving about 118571.43. This is the scalar subquery `(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee)` that runs once.

Step 2: The service filters to salaries strictly above 118571.43. That keeps Priya (150000), Neha (140000), Sanjay (130000), Kiran (130000), and Rajesh (120000). Amit (110000) and Low Earner (50000) are excluded. This is the `WHERE salary > avg`.

To find the top five employees earning above the average salary I first compute the overall average with a scalar subquery and compare each row to it, then take the top five. The LIMIT version is `SELECT name, salary FROM employee WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee) ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5`, or `SELECT TOP 5` on SQL Server. I also remember that AVG ignores NULL salaries and that salary is a decimal type. The line I remember is: filter to above the average, then LIMIT 5 for speed or RANK up to five for fair tie handling.

answers.question: Write a query to find duplicate customer emails (`GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`), and explain why the application-level `if (!emailExists) insert` check is NOT enough under concurrency and must be backed by a DB `UNIQUE` constraint (the app validates, the database enforces).
answers.shortTitle: Duplicate Customer Emails and Why App-Level Checks Need a DB UNIQUE Constraint

s1_definition.profdef: Finding duplicate emails groups by a normalized email and keeps groups with a count above one. The deeper point is that an application-level "check-then-insert" (`if (!emailExists) insert`) is a race condition: between the check and the insert, another thread or node can insert the same email, so both succeed. Only a database `UNIQUE` constraint, which the engine enforces atomically at write time, guarantees no duplicates. The app validates for a friendly message; the database enforces for correctness.
s1_definition.analogy: Two people walk up to two different counters at the National Bank of India at the exact same second, both wanting to register the email rajesh@x.com. Each teller checks "is this email taken?" — both see "no" because neither registration is saved yet — and both say "go ahead." Now the email exists twice. The only fix is a rule stamped on the ledger itself that physically refuses a second identical email, no matter how many tellers are working. That ledger rule is the `UNIQUE` constraint.
s1_definition.oneliner: `GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` finds dupes, but the app's check-then-insert races under concurrency — only a DB `UNIQUE` constraint truly prevents duplicates.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding duplicate emails groups by a normalized email and keeps groups with a count above one. The deeper point is that an application-level "check-then-insert" (`if (!emailExists) insert`) is a race condition: between the check and the insert, another thread or node can insert the same email, so both succeed. Only a database `UNIQUE` constraint, which the engine enforces atomically at write time, guarantees no duplicates. The app validates for a friendly message; the database enforces for correctness.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two people walk up to two different counters at the National Bank of India at the exact same second, both wanting to register the email rajesh@x.com. Each teller checks "is this email taken?" — both see "no" because neither registration is saved yet — and both say "go ahead." Now the email exists twice. The only fix is a rule stamped on the ledger itself that physically refuses a second identical email, no matter how many tellers are working. That ledger rule is the `UNIQUE` constraint.

**One line to remember:** `GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` finds dupes, but the app's check-then-insert races under concurrency — only a DB `UNIQUE` constraint truly prevents duplicates.

sections.s2_technical:
The detection query is the standard duplicate pattern, with normalization because emails are case-insensitive in practice:

```sql
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS norm_email, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM customers
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

`LOWER(TRIM(email))` folds `Rajesh@X.com` and ` rajesh@x.com ` into the same key so near-duplicates are caught, grouping buckets by that key, and `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` keeps only the repeated ones.

The core teaching point is why this situation arises and how to prevent it. A very common but broken pattern in application code is check-then-act:

```java
if (!customerRepo.existsByEmail(email)) {   // step 1: check
    customerRepo.insert(new Customer(email)); // step 2: insert
}
```

This looks safe for a single thread, but under concurrency it has a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race. Imagine two requests arrive simultaneously with the same email. Thread A runs the check and sees the email does not exist. Before A inserts, Thread B also runs the check and also sees it does not exist, because A has not committed yet. Both then insert, and you have two rows with the same email. This is not a rare theoretical case; at scale, with retries and double-clicks, it happens regularly. Raising the database isolation level does not reliably fix it either, because the two transactions are inserting new rows that each other cannot "see," so even SERIALIZABLE may allow it unless there is a constraint or you use explicit locking.

The correct, durable fix is a database `UNIQUE` constraint:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ADD CONSTRAINT uq_customers_email UNIQUE (email);
```

The database enforces uniqueness atomically as part of the write. If two concurrent inserts race, the first to commit wins and the second fails with a unique-violation error, which the application catches and turns into a friendly "email already registered" message. The application-level check is still useful — it gives a fast, friendly response in the common non-racing case and avoids an exception on every normal duplicate — but it is an optimization, not the guarantee. The guarantee lives in the database.

Senior-level details: for case-insensitive uniqueness you either store emails already lowercased, or create a functional unique index `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON customers (LOWER(email))`, or use a case-insensitive type like PostgreSQL's `citext`; a plain `UNIQUE(email)` would still allow `A@x.com` and `a@x.com` as distinct. The robust write pattern is "try the insert, catch the unique violation" (optimistic), or use an upsert like `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING`. The principle generalizes far beyond emails: any invariant that must never be violated (unique account numbers, one active loan per customer, non-negative balance) belongs as a database constraint, because the database is the single serialization point that all concurrent clients funnel through. The mantra is: the application validates, the database enforces.

The fix had two parts: a detection query to find existing duplicate emails for cleanup, and a `UNIQUE` constraint so it can never recur.

Step 3: Against the enforced store the first `registerEnforced` inserts successfully, holding the lock during the atomic insert. The second `registerEnforced` runs the enforced insert, finds the email already present inside the same atomic operation, and throws a unique-violation, which the service catches and turns into a friendly warning.

Step 4: The enforced store always ends with exactly one row for the email, regardless of concurrency, because the database (simulated by the synchronized atomic insert) is the single serialization point.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicate emails I group by a normalized email and keep groups with a count above one: `SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)), COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`, normalizing so case and whitespace variations are caught. But the more important part of this question is why they exist. An application check like `if (!emailExists) insert` is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race: under concurrency two requests with the same email both run the existence check before either commits, both see "not present," and both insert, producing a duplicate. Raising the isolation level does not reliably help because each transaction is inserting a new row the other cannot see yet. The only robust fix is a database UNIQUE constraint, because the database is the single serialization point that every concurrent client funnels through, and it enforces uniqueness atomically at write time.

In our National Bank of India registration flow a customer double-clicked submit on a slow connection, two near-simultaneous requests both passed the check-then-insert, and two accounts ended up sharing one email, which later broke password reset. I cleaned up the existing duplicates with the detection query and added a case-insensitive unique index on the lowercased email so it can never recur, and I kept the application-level check only as a friendly-message optimization for the common non-racing case while catching the unique-violation for the race. The principle I always state is that the application validates but the database enforces, and that any invariant that must never be violated — unique account numbers, one active loan per customer, a non-negative balance — belongs as a database constraint. The line I remember is: the app's check-then-insert races, so back every uniqueness rule with a DB UNIQUE constraint.

answers.question: Write a query to return the latest order (full row) per customer and the most expensive order per customer (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC)` → filter `= 1`), and the top-3 orders/earners per group (`<= 3`).
answers.shortTitle: Latest and Most Expensive Order per Customer, and Top-3 per Group — ROW_NUMBER

s1_definition.profdef: "One row per group" problems are solved with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_key ORDER BY sort_key)`, which numbers rows within each partition starting at one, then filtering to row number one gives the top record per group. For the latest order you order by `created_at DESC, id DESC`; for the most expensive you order by `amount DESC`. Changing the filter to row number `<= 3` returns the top three per group.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants, for each customer, their most recent order and their biggest order. Imagine making one stack of each customer's orders. For "latest," sort each stack newest-on-top and take the top slip. For "most expensive," sort each stack biggest-amount-on-top and take the top slip. `PARTITION BY customer` makes the per-customer stacks, `ORDER BY` decides what "top" means, `ROW_NUMBER` tags each slip 1, 2, 3, and keeping tag 1 gives the top — or keeping 1 through 3 gives the top three.
s1_definition.oneliner: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY ...)` then filter `= 1` for the top row per customer, or `<= 3` for the top three.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** "One row per group" problems are solved with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_key ORDER BY sort_key)`, which numbers rows within each partition starting at one, then filtering to row number one gives the top record per group. For the latest order you order by `created_at DESC, id DESC`; for the most expensive you order by `amount DESC`. Changing the filter to row number `<= 3` returns the top three per group.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants, for each customer, their most recent order and their biggest order. Imagine making one stack of each customer's orders. For "latest," sort each stack newest-on-top and take the top slip. For "most expensive," sort each stack biggest-amount-on-top and take the top slip. `PARTITION BY customer` makes the per-customer stacks, `ORDER BY` decides what "top" means, `ROW_NUMBER` tags each slip 1, 2, 3, and keeping tag 1 gives the top — or keeping 1 through 3 gives the top three.

**One line to remember:** `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY ...)` then filter `= 1` for the top row per customer, or `<= 3` for the top three.

sections.s2_technical:
The window function `ROW_NUMBER()` is the workhorse for "pick the top-N rows within each group." `PARTITION BY customer_id` restarts the numbering for each customer, and the `ORDER BY` inside the `OVER` clause decides which row is number one. Because window functions cannot be used directly in a `WHERE` clause, you wrap the query in a subquery or CTE and filter on the computed number outside.

The latest order per customer, as full rows, with a deterministic tie-break:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT o.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM orders o
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
```

Ordering by `created_at DESC` puts the newest order first; adding `, id DESC` is important because two orders could share the same timestamp, and without a tie-breaker `ROW_NUMBER` would pick one arbitrarily and the result could change between runs. The `id DESC` makes it deterministic — pick the newest, and if tied, the one inserted last.

The most expensive order per customer is the same shape with a different sort key:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT o.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY total_amount DESC, id DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM orders o
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
```

The top-three per group simply changes the filter from `= 1` to `<= 3`:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT o.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total_amount DESC, id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders o
) t
WHERE rn <= 3;
```

The critical senior distinction is `ROW_NUMBER` versus `RANK`/`DENSE_RANK` for top-N. `ROW_NUMBER` always gives exactly N rows per group even if there are ties, picking arbitrarily among tied rows (unless your tie-breaker makes it deterministic). If you want "top 3 including everyone tied at third place," you use `DENSE_RANK() <= 3` instead, which may return more than three rows. For "latest" there is usually no meaningful tie beyond the timestamp, so `ROW_NUMBER` with an id tie-breaker is ideal; for "top earners" where ties are meaningful you often prefer `RANK`/`DENSE_RANK`.

Performance matters at scale: a composite index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)` lets the engine produce the ordered partitions efficiently for the latest-order query, and `(customer_id, total_amount DESC)` for the most-expensive query. These top-N-per-group queries are extremely common for dashboards (latest transaction per account, biggest trade per client), so recognizing the `ROW_NUMBER`/`PARTITION BY`/filter pattern is a core SQL skill.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's relationship managers need a customer dashboard that shows, per customer, their latest order (to see recent activity) and their single most expensive order (to gauge value), plus their top three orders by amount for a quick history. Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) each have several orders. A previous version used `GROUP BY customer_id` with `MAX(created_at)`, but that returned only the timestamp, not the full order row (id, amount, items), so the dashboard could not link to the actual order.

This is the classic `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` top-N-per-group pattern. Our mini-project models an `Order`, a repository, and an `OrderAnalyticsService` with methods for latest-per-customer, most-expensive-per-customer, and top-three-per-customer, mirroring the three queries and returning full rows.

The code will contain: an `Order` class with id, customer, createdAt, and amount; an `OrderRepository`; an `OrderAnalyticsService` with the three methods using the window-function logic; and a `Demo` printing each result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five orders — SAV2001 has orders 1 (Jan, 12000), 2 (Feb, 50000), 3 (Mar, 30000); CUR3001 has orders 4 (Jan, 90000), 5 (Feb, 20000).

Step 1: The service partitions orders by customer, building SAV2001's list of three and CUR3001's list of two. This is `PARTITION BY customer_id` — the per-customer stacks.

Step 2: For the latest order, within each partition it sorts by created_at descending (tie-broken by id descending) and takes the first. SAV2001's newest is the March order (id 3); CUR3001's newest is the February order (id 5). This is `ROW_NUMBER() ... ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC` filtered to one. Full rows are returned, not just timestamps.

Step 3: For the most expensive order, it re-sorts each partition by amount descending and takes the first. SAV2001's biggest is 50000 (id 2); CUR3001's biggest is 90000 (id 4). This is the same pattern with a different sort key.

Step 4: For the top three by amount, it sorts each partition by amount descending and takes up to three. SAV2001 returns 50000, 30000, 12000 (all three it has); CUR3001 returns 90000, 20000 (it only has two). This is the `<= 3` filter.

Step 5: The application prints all three result sets, each carrying full order rows the dashboard can link to.

sections.s6_takeaway:
For "one row per group" problems I reach for `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ...)` and filter on the computed number in an outer query, because window functions cannot be used directly in WHERE. For the latest order per customer I order by `created_at DESC, id DESC` and keep row number one, returning the full order row rather than just a timestamp; the `id DESC` tie-breaker makes it deterministic when two orders share a timestamp. For the most expensive order I keep the same shape but order by `total_amount DESC, id DESC` and keep row number one. For the top three per group I change the filter from equal to one to less than or equal to three.

In our National Bank of India relationship-manager dashboard we needed each customer's latest order and single biggest order, plus their top three by amount. An earlier version used GROUP BY with MAX on the timestamp, which returned only the timestamp and not the full order row, so the dashboard could not link to the actual order — the window-function approach returns the whole row, which fixed it. The senior distinction I always state is ROW_NUMBER versus RANK and DENSE_RANK: ROW_NUMBER gives exactly N rows per group and is arbitrary on ties unless I add a tie-breaker, RANK gives tied rows the same number and then skips, and DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number without skipping, so for a fair "top 3 including everyone tied at third" I would switch to DENSE_RANK. I also add composite indexes on the partition and sort columns so these queries stay fast. The line I remember is: ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the group, ordered by the key, filtered to one for the top row or three for the top three.

answers.question: Write a query to find customers who ordered on at least two consecutive days (reduce to distinct customer/day, `LAG(order_date)` within each customer, then keep rows where `DATEDIFF(order_date, previous_date) = 1`).
answers.shortTitle: Customers Who Ordered on at Least Two Consecutive Days — LAG and DATEDIFF

s1_definition.profdef: This is a gaps-and-islands style problem. You first reduce orders to distinct (customer, day) pairs so multiple orders on the same day count once. Then within each customer, ordered by day, you use `LAG(order_date)` to look at the previous order day on the same row, and you keep rows where the current day is exactly one day after the previous day. Any customer with such a row ordered on two consecutive days.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find loyal customers who placed an order two days in a row. Priya takes each customer's list of order days, removes repeats so each day appears once, sorts them, and walks down the list asking "is this day exactly one after the day above it?" If yes even once, that customer is loyal. The "day above it" is `LAG`, and "exactly one day after" is the date difference equalling one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Distinct customer/day, then `LAG(day)` within each customer ordered by day, and keep where today minus the previous day equals one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a gaps-and-islands style problem. You first reduce orders to distinct (customer, day) pairs so multiple orders on the same day count once. Then within each customer, ordered by day, you use `LAG(order_date)` to look at the previous order day on the same row, and you keep rows where the current day is exactly one day after the previous day. Any customer with such a row ordered on two consecutive days.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to find loyal customers who placed an order two days in a row. Priya takes each customer's list of order days, removes repeats so each day appears once, sorts them, and walks down the list asking "is this day exactly one after the day above it?" If yes even once, that customer is loyal. The "day above it" is `LAG`, and "exactly one day after" is the date difference equalling one.

**One line to remember:** Distinct customer/day, then `LAG(day)` within each customer ordered by day, and keep where today minus the previous day equals one.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem has three clean stages. Stage one is deduplication: a customer might place several orders on the same day, which should count as one day, so you reduce to distinct (customer_id, order_day). Casting the timestamp to a date and selecting distinct does this:

```sql
WITH days AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS d
    FROM orders
)
```

Stage two uses the `LAG` window function to bring each customer's previous order day onto the current row. `LAG(d) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY d)` returns, for each row, the day value from the row immediately before it within the same customer, in day order:

```sql
, with_prev AS (
    SELECT customer_id, d,
           LAG(d) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY d) AS prev_d
    FROM days
)
```

Stage three keeps the rows where the current day is exactly one day after the previous day. In MySQL this is `DATEDIFF(d, prev_d) = 1`; in PostgreSQL you write `d - prev_d = 1` (date subtraction yields an integer number of days). A customer who appears in the result ordered on two consecutive days:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
FROM with_prev
WHERE d - prev_d = 1;      -- PostgreSQL; MySQL: DATEDIFF(d, prev_d) = 1
```

Why `LAG` rather than a self-join? You could self-join the days table to itself on `d = prev.d + 1`, and that works, but `LAG` is cleaner, reads top to bottom, and is usually more efficient because it is a single ordered pass rather than a join. The `DISTINCT` at the end collapses customers who have several consecutive-day pairs to one row.

Senior nuances. First, the deduplication to distinct days is essential — without it, two orders on the same day with a `LAG` could produce a zero-day difference and confuse the logic. Second, the first row of each customer has a `NULL` previous day (nothing precedes it), and `NULL - prev` or `DATEDIFF` with NULL yields NULL, which the `= 1` comparison treats as not-true, so those rows are naturally excluded — no special handling needed. Third, if the question were "three consecutive days" you would either chain two `LAG`s or use the classic gaps-and-islands trick of subtracting a dense row number from the date to form islands and then group. Fourth, time zones matter: "a day" is defined in some zone, so for the bank you cast in the reporting zone (`order_date AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'`) before taking the date. For performance an index on `(customer_id, order_date)` supports the partitioned ordering.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India runs a "streak" loyalty perk for customers who transact on consecutive days. The marketing team wants the list of customers who ordered on at least two days in a row. Rajesh (SAV2001) ordered on Jan 1 and Jan 2 (consecutive) and again on Jan 5. Priya (CUR3001) ordered on Jan 1 and Jan 3 (a gap, not consecutive). So Rajesh qualifies and Priya does not. A naive approach that just counted orders per customer wrongly flagged Priya because she had multiple orders — but they were not on consecutive days.

This exercises distinct-days plus `LAG` plus a one-day difference. Our mini-project models an `Order`, a repository, and a `StreakService` that reduces to distinct days, compares each day to the previous within a customer, and returns customers with a consecutive-day pair.

The code will contain: an `Order` class, an `OrderRepository`, a `StreakService.customersWithConsecutiveDays()` method implementing the three stages, and a `Demo` printing the qualifying customers.

Input data: SAV2001 ordered Jan 1, Jan 2, Jan 5; CUR3001 ordered Jan 1, Jan 3.

Step 1: The service reduces each customer's orders to distinct days. SAV2001 becomes {Jan 1, Jan 2, Jan 5}; CUR3001 becomes {Jan 1, Jan 3}. This is the `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE)` stage. Using a `TreeSet` both deduplicates and sorts.

Step 2: For SAV2001 the service walks the sorted days comparing each to the previous (the `LAG`). Jan 1 has no previous. Jan 2 minus Jan 1 equals one day — a consecutive pair — so SAV2001 qualifies immediately. This is `LAG(d)` plus the one-day difference check.

Step 3: For CUR3001 the service walks {Jan 1, Jan 3}. Jan 1 has no previous. Jan 3 minus Jan 1 equals two days, not one, so there is no consecutive pair. CUR3001 does not qualify. The NULL previous on the first row is naturally skipped, matching how SQL's `= 1` treats NULL as not-true.

Step 4: The qualifying list contains only SAV2001. The final `DISTINCT` has no effect here since each customer is added at most once, but it mirrors the SQL that collapses multiple streak pairs per customer.

Step 5: The application prints SAV2001 as the sole streak customer, correctly excluding Priya despite her having multiple orders.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find customers who ordered on at least two consecutive days I do three things. First I reduce the orders to distinct customer-and-day pairs, because several orders on the same day should count as one day, which I get with `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE)`. Second, within each customer ordered by day, I bring the previous order day onto the current row with `LAG(d) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY d)`. Third, I keep the rows where today minus the previous day equals one, which in PostgreSQL is `d - prev_d = 1` and in MySQL is `DATEDIFF(d, prev_d) = 1`, then select distinct customers. Any customer who appears ordered on two consecutive days.

In our National Bank of India streak loyalty perk, marketing wanted customers who transacted on consecutive days. Rajesh ordered on January 1 and 2, so he qualified, while Priya ordered on January 1 and 3, a gap, so she did not — and crucially a naive count of orders per customer would have wrongly flagged Priya just for having multiple orders. The LAG approach compares adjacent days, which is exactly the right test. The senior points I add are that the first row of each customer has a NULL previous day that the equals-one comparison naturally excludes, that I prefer LAG over a self-join because it is a single ordered pass and reads cleanly, that for three-or-more consecutive days I would use the gaps-and-islands trick of subtracting a row number from the date to form islands, and that "a day" is time-zone dependent so I cast in the bank's reporting zone first. The line I remember is: distinct customer-day, LAG the previous day within each customer, and keep where the difference is one.

answers.question: Write a query to find customers (or users) who have BOTH state A and state B (e.g. a completed AND a cancelled order) using conditional aggregation in one grouped pass.
answers.shortTitle: Customers With BOTH State A and State B — Conditional Aggregation

s1_definition.profdef: To find entities that have at least one row of state A and at least one row of state B, you group by the entity and use conditional aggregation in the `HAVING` clause: `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) > 0`. This does it in one grouped pass over the table, avoiding two separate queries intersected together.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants customers who have both a completed order and a cancelled order — a signal worth investigating. Priya groups all orders by customer, and for each customer she asks two questions in one pass: "does this customer have at least one completed order?" and "at least one cancelled order?" Only customers who answer yes to both make the list. Counting the completed ones and the cancelled ones separately within the same group is conditional aggregation.
s1_definition.oneliner: Group by the customer and use `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status='A') > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status='B') > 0` — both states proven in a single pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** To find entities that have at least one row of state A and at least one row of state B, you group by the entity and use conditional aggregation in the `HAVING` clause: `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) > 0`. This does it in one grouped pass over the table, avoiding two separate queries intersected together.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants customers who have both a completed order and a cancelled order — a signal worth investigating. Priya groups all orders by customer, and for each customer she asks two questions in one pass: "does this customer have at least one completed order?" and "at least one cancelled order?" Only customers who answer yes to both make the list. Counting the completed ones and the cancelled ones separately within the same group is conditional aggregation.

**One line to remember:** Group by the customer and use `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status='A') > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status='B') > 0` — both states proven in a single pass.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach runs two queries — "customers with a completed order" and "customers with a cancelled order" — and intersects them, or uses two `EXISTS` subqueries. That works but scans the table multiple times. Conditional aggregation does it in a single grouped pass, which is cleaner and usually faster.

The technique puts a `CASE` expression inside an aggregate. `COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END)` counts only the rows where the condition is true, because `CASE` returns `NULL` otherwise and `COUNT` ignores NULLs. So within each customer's group, this expression tells you how many completed orders they have:

```sql
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END) > 0
   AND COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 END) > 0;
```

`GROUP BY customer_id` makes one group per customer, the first conditional count must be above zero (at least one completed order exists), and the second must be above zero (at least one cancelled order exists). The `AND` requires both, so only customers satisfying both states survive. This reads the table once.

You can equivalently use `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` or, in PostgreSQL, the compact `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'COMPLETED')`, which is the modern standard-SQL filtered aggregate and reads very clearly:

```sql
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'COMPLETED') > 0
   AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'CANCELLED') > 0;
```

The same pattern generalizes nicely. "Customers with A but NOT B" becomes `HAVING COUNT(... A ...) > 0 AND COUNT(... B ...) = 0`. "Customers with all of A, B and C" just adds more conditions. "At least two of three states" can use a sum of booleans. This flexibility is why conditional aggregation is preferred over intersecting multiple queries once you need anything beyond the simplest case.

Senior nuances: the conditional counts can also be projected in the `SELECT` to report how many of each state a customer has, which the two-query approach cannot do in one shot. Watch the difference between `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)` (counts matching rows) and `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` (counts all rows, because 0 is not NULL) — the `ELSE 0` version is wrong for counting and must be paired with `SUM`, not `COUNT`. For performance an index on `(customer_id, status)` supports the grouping and the conditional filters. And when status values come from user input, keep them controlled (an enum or lookup) so the CASE conditions stay reliable.

Problem — National Bank of India's risk team wants to flag customers who have both a COMPLETED order and a CANCELLED order, because that pattern can indicate testing stolen cards (complete one, cancel another) and warrants a review. Rajesh (SAV2001) has one completed and one cancelled order — he should be flagged. Priya (CUR3001) has two completed orders but no cancellation — she should not. An earlier approach ran two separate queries and intersected them in application code, which was slow and hard to extend when risk added a third state.

This exercises conditional aggregation in a single grouped pass. Our mini-project models an `Order` with a status, a repository, and a `RiskReviewService` that returns customers having both states using one pass of conditional counts.

The code will contain: an `Order` class with a `status`, an `OrderRepository`, a `RiskReviewService.customersWithBothStates()` method implementing the conditional-aggregation HAVING logic, and a `Demo` printing the flagged customers.

Input data: four orders — SAV2001 has one COMPLETED and one CANCELLED; CUR3001 has two COMPLETED.

Step 1: The service groups orders by customer, preparing a two-slot counter per customer: one slot for state A (COMPLETED) and one for state B (CANCELLED). This is the `GROUP BY customer_id` plus the two conditional counts.

Step 2: It scans every order once. SAV2001's COMPLETED order increments slot A to 1; SAV2001's CANCELLED order increments slot B to 1. Step 3: It applies the HAVING test: keep customers where both slots are above zero. SAV2001 has A=1 and B=1, so both are positive and he is flagged. CUR3001 has A=2 and B=0, so the cancelled condition fails and she is not flagged.

Step 4: The flagged list contains only SAV2001. Note the table was read just once — no intersection of two separate queries.

Step 5: The application prints SAV2001 for the risk team to review.
